de/capabilityGate.json::capabilityGate.d: This is part of the production system. It is shown here so you can see what Provisa does, but it is not available in the sandbox.

An environment is a complete, separately governed copy of your model: its sources, tables, policies, masking rules and grants. Teams change the model in dev, review it in staging and serve from prod, merging one environment into the next with a diff, an approval and an undoable history.

Your sandbox is one of these environments, made for you alone. Creating, merging, deploying and retiring them belongs to the organization that owns them, so this page is shown for reference and acts on nothing.

Invite the person into the root organization from its Team page.
They sign in and redeem the invitation, which makes them a member of root.
Assign them the platform_admin role in root, which confers deployment-wide administration.

Signing in made you this deployment's platform_admin. You hold every capability here, and nobody else can claim the role now. You are also the administrator of the root organization, which already carries the demo sources, tables, and domains.

From the next sign-in onward, anyone who authenticates creates their own organization. They are never made a platform administrator by signing in, and inviting people into their org is their own work as its org_admin.

de/replicateSelect.json::replicateSelect: Live if possible: read directly from the source; replicated only where the engine cannot read it directly. Always: always from the replica, the only setting that is a guarantee.

Always, source read only on schedule: reads always come from the replica and a query never causes the source to be read; the scheduler refreshes the replica on the off-peak window, the Cache TTL or the change probe, and at least one of the three is required.

When reads of this source's tables come from their replicas, copies in the engine's store refreshed on each table's timeliness settings. A table with no setting of its own uses this one. Default: the global threshold.
When this table's reads come from its replica, a copy in the engine's store refreshed on the table's timeliness settings. Default: the source's setting, or the global threshold when it has none.
Live if possible cannot be combined with load protection, because a load-protected table is never read live.

Rules name roles, so to change what someone can see, change the role they hold.

A row-level security rule is a SQL predicate bound to one role and one scope. The server ANDs it into the query before execution, on reads and writes and on every surface, so a role sees only the rows its rule permits whichever client it uses.

Every other permission is written against a role. Its capabilities decide which operations it may run, and its domain access decides which parts of the model it can reach. de/settings.json::settings.auth.login_th: How long a locked-out account is refused. Guarded because shortening it weakens the brake on password guessing.
How many failed sign-ins within the window lock an account out. Guarded because raising it weakens the brake on password guessing.
How far back failed sign-ins are counted. Guarded because shortening it weakens the brake on password guessing.

de/settings.json::settings.bolt.allowed_: The web sites allowed to open a Bolt connection from a browser; none are allowed until listed. Guarded because each entry lets that site drive the port.
de/settings.json::settings.bolt.recv_tim: The hint a Bolt (Neo4j) client is given for how long to wait for a reply.
de/settings.json::settings.bootstrap.con: The config file this deployment was started on. Not editable: it is read before stored settings can be.
de/settings.json::settings.bootstrap.dat: The folder the deployment keeps its files in. Not editable: it is read before stored settings can be.
de/settings.json::settings.bootstrap.dem: Whether the deployment was started in demo mode. Set by the launcher; not editable.
de/settings.json::settings.bootstrap.hom: The deployment's home folder for certificates and local stores. Not editable: it is read before stored settings can be.
de/settings.json::settings.cache.default: How long a cached result is kept when nothing more specific says; an organization can set its own. Restart required for the deployment default.
de/settings.json::settings.cache.enabled: Whether query results may be cached at all. Restart required because the cache store is built at start.
de/settings.json::settings.cache.redis_e: Whether this is a desktop launch running on the built-in Redis. Set by the launcher; not editable.
de/settings.json::settings.cache.redis_o: The password given to each organization's own Redis account when it is created. Secret; guarded.
de/settings.json::settings.cache.redis_u: The address of the Redis server used for caching and rate limiting; unset uses the built-in one. Secret because it can carry a password; restart required because connections are opened at start; guarded.
de/settings.json::settings.codesource.du: The memory a code source's DuckDB answers a statement in. Past it, the statement spills to disk.

The most a code source's DuckDB spills to disk. A statement that needs more is refused, naming this setting. A built image enforces it only when its spill volume is sized to this cap with the platform's quota. A code source in dev mode spills into the data directory with no bound.
The threads a code source's DuckDB answers its statements on.
de/settings.json::settings.codesource.he: How often each Provisa process asks a connector's host for its health, and shows the result on the source. A host that restarted is noticed on the next poll, which runs its on-start function again.
de/settings.json::settings.codesource.wo: How long a code source's worker, or an organization's preflight worker, may go unused before Provisa ends its process. The next call starts a new one.
de/settings.json::settings.commands.allo: On: python and script commands may be registered and called. Each runs with the server's own access to its memory, credentials, files and network, and its code does not travel with the model. Off by default; use a code resolver instead.
de/settings.json::settings.compiler.comp: How long a compiled query plan is reused before it is rebuilt. Restart required because each worker reads it when it builds its cache.
de/settings.json::settings.concurrency.b: The number of threads each worker process uses for background work; restart required because the pool is sized once at start.
de/settings.json::settings.concurrency.c: Threads each worker process keeps for health checks and the admin and sign-in API, so heavy data traffic cannot make a worker unreachable to its orchestrator or its administrators.
de/settings.json::settings.concurrency.f: The most Arrow Flight streams one worker process runs at once; more wait for a slot. Restart required because the slots are created at start.
de/settings.json::settings.concurrency.g: The most gRPC calls one worker process serves at once; more are refused. Restart required because it sizes the gRPC server's thread pool.
de/settings.json::settings.concurrency.r: The most requests one worker process runs at once; more wait for a free thread. Restart required because the limit is fixed when the worker starts.
de/settings.json::settings.concurrency.s: The most streamed responses and open WebSockets one worker process holds at once, subscriptions included. Each one waits on its client rather than using a core, so this is kept apart from the request threads.
de/settings.json::settings.config.reload: How often each worker checks whether the model or a setting has changed, and reloads it if so. A change made in one worker reaches the others within this time.
de/settings.json::settings.connectors.cl: A folder holding a Cloud Inventory server bundle built for this host, with its launcher under bin/. Empty uses the pinned release. A folder without the launcher stops the server from starting, naming this setting.
de/settings.json::settings.connectors.fi: A folder holding a File Crawler server bundle built for this host, with its launcher under bin/. Empty uses the pinned release. A folder without the launcher stops the server from starting, naming this setting.
de/settings.json::settings.connectors.go: A folder holding a AskAmerica server bundle built for this host, with its launcher under bin/. Empty uses the pinned release. A folder without the launcher stops the server from starting, naming this setting.
de/settings.json::settings.connectors.ji: A folder holding a Jira server bundle built for this host, with its launcher under bin/. Empty uses the pinned release. A folder without the launcher stops the server from starting, naming this setting.
de/settings.json::settings.connectors.sa: A folder holding a Salesforce server bundle built for this host, with its launcher under bin/. Empty uses the pinned release. A folder without the launcher stops the server from starting, naming this setting.
de/settings.json::settings.connectors.se: A folder holding a ServiceNow server bundle built for this host, with its launcher under bin/. Empty uses the pinned release. A folder without the launcher stops the server from starting, naming this setting.
de/settings.json::settings.connectors.sh: A folder holding a SharePoint server bundle built for this host, with its launcher under bin/. Empty uses the pinned release. A folder without the launcher stops the server from starting, naming this setting.
de/settings.json::settings.connectors.sp: A folder holding a Splunk server bundle built for this host, with its launcher under bin/. Empty uses the pinned release. A folder without the launcher stops the server from starting, naming this setting.
de/settings.json::settings.control_plane: The organization this deployment starts as. Not editable: it is read before stored settings can be.
The database that holds accounts, organizations and these settings. Not editable: the deployment needs it to find its stored settings.
The largest number of control-plane database connections each worker opens. Not editable: the pool is opened before stored settings can be read.
The smallest number of control-plane database connections each worker keeps. Not editable: the pool is opened before stored settings can be read.
The database that holds each organization's configuration. Not editable: the deployment needs it to find its stored settings.
de/settings.json::settings.demo.setup_co: The named demos whose setup has run against this deployment. A demo listed here is not set up again when it starts; remove it to set it up again on its next start.
de/settings.json::settings.embedding.hub: The Hugging Face hub a local embedding model is downloaded from, such as a mirror inside your network. Applies to the next model download.
de/settings.json::settings.engine.duckdb: The most memory any DuckDB engine of this deployment may use. Past it, a query spills to disk or is refused. Unset: DuckDB's own limit, most of the host's memory.
de/settings.json::settings.engine.exchan: Where the engine keeps intermediate data for fault-tolerant execution. Takes effect when the engine restarts.
de/settings.json::settings.engine.fault_: Whether the engine retries failed parts of a query instead of failing the whole query. Takes effect when the engine restarts.
The memory reserved per task when fault-tolerant execution is on. Takes effect when the engine restarts.
de/settings.json::settings.engine.jvm_he: The memory given to the federation engine's Java process. Takes effect when the engine restarts.
de/settings.json::settings.engine.query_: The most memory one query may use across the engine cluster. Takes effect when the engine restarts.
The most memory one query may use on a single engine node. Takes effect when the engine restarts.
The most memory one query may use in total, including system memory. Takes effect when the engine restarts.
de/settings.json::settings.engine.ready_: How long startup waits for the federation engine to become ready before failing.
de/settings.json::settings.engine.trino_: The coordinator's pinned address on the engine network, in its lower half: Trino finds its coordinator by IP alone when traffic between nodes is encrypted. Applies at the next start.

The network the engine's containers share while traffic between engine nodes is encrypted. The coordinator's address is in its lower half; every other container gets one from the upper half. Applies at the next start.

Trino's coordinator and workers require HTTPS between them. Off by default: their traffic stays on the deployment's private network, authenticated by a shared secret. Turn it on where a compliance or zero-trust requirement asks for encryption inside the deployment; shuffle-heavy queries (joins, aggregations, window functions) run 10% to over 100% slower. Applies at the next start.
de/settings.json::settings.fakes.key.hel: The secret every fake value is derived from, the same on every node and region. It is created at the platform's first start. Changing it changes every fake value; guarded, and a restart is required.
de/settings.json::settings.fakes.leak_ra: The share of a sensitive column's sampled values its fake may leave equal to the real value before the leak-rate check marks the fake inadequate. 0 fails a fake that leaves any value unchanged.
de/settings.json::settings.graph.depth_l: The most hops a Cypher variable-length path or a SPARQL property path walks when the query sets no bound of its own. A Cypher path keeps no relationship twice and, if it would go further, fails by name; a SPARQL result cut at this depth says it was cut. Very large by default (1000).
de/settings.json::settings.graph.union_l: A SPARQL pattern whose predicate is a variable reads every mapped predicate it could match, one branch each. A query needing more branches than this is refused, naming the limit.
Most predicates a variable predicate covers
de/settings.json::settings.grpc.allow_un: Lets gRPC clients list the services of a deployment that has no authentication. Restart required; guarded because it exposes the service surface.
de/settings.json::settings.grpc.max_mess: The largest single gRPC message the server sends or accepts; restart required because it is a server option set when the gRPC server is built.
de/settings.json::settings.hot_tables.au: A table with no more rows than this is kept whole in the hot cache (Redis) and read from there. Restart required.
de/settings.json::settings.hot_tables.ma: The most bytes the hot cache holds for one table; a larger table is read live instead. Restart required.
The most rows the hot cache holds for one table. Unset uses the hot table size limit. Restart required.
de/settings.json::settings.hot_tables.re: How often tables in the hot cache are reloaded from their source. Unset uses the default materialized view lifetime. Restart required.
de/settings.json::settings.kaggle.api_to: The token Kaggle searches and dataset downloads sign in with: the token itself, or a reference to a secret you created, such as ${secret:NAME}.
de/settings.json::settings.limits.defaul: The most rows a query returns when the caller sets no limit of its own.
de/settings.json::settings.limits.engine: How long the federation engine may run one query before it is cancelled.
de/settings.json::settings.limits.max_qu: The highest complexity score one statement may have, for every role. A role may set a lower limit of its own. Leave unset for no limit.
de/settings.json::settings.limits.reques: How long a request may run before it is cancelled, for any transport without a value of its own.
The request time limit for each transport on its own; a transport left empty uses the default. Flight ships at 3600 seconds and pgwire at 300.
de/settings.json::settings.limits.retry_: How long a failed query keeps being retried before the error is returned; 0 turns retries off.
de/settings.json::settings.logs.allowed_: The directories a Logs source's files may be in, once their links are followed; by default /var/log. Add one, such as ~/Library/Logs, to read the server's own files under it into tables. A sandbox organization, and on a server of many organizations every organization but the deployment's own, reads no file of the server's own outside its own folder but those its demo's sources name, whatever this says.
Directories log files may be read from
de/settings.json::settings.logs.max_line: A longer record keeps its first bytes as its raw text, and its parse error says it was too long.
de/settings.json::settings.logs.preview_: A JSON-lines or logfmt source's columns are the fields its files' first lines name. More lines find fields that appear rarely, and take longer to read.
Lines read to find a log's columns
de/settings.json::settings.mail.mailboxe: How many mailboxes a source of an organization's mailboxes reads at the same time. More shortens a build and asks more of the mail service's limit for the whole application.
de/settings.json::settings.mail.throttle: When Microsoft or Google asks a replica's read to wait, it waits and goes on. This is the most the waits of one request may add up to, in seconds; a longer one fails the build, which is tried again later. Raise it to ride out long throttles; to be throttled less, lower Mailboxes read at once.
Longest wait when a mail service is throttling
de/settings.json::settings.materialized_: How long a materialized view is used before it is refreshed, when it sets no lifetime of its own. Restart required.
de/settings.json::settings.mcp.chat_mode: The model the built-in chat uses, overriding each organization's own choice.
de/settings.json::settings.mcp.external_: The MCP address shown to users when the deployment sits behind a proxy.
de/settings.json::settings.mcp.host.help: The network address the MCP server binds; 127.0.0.1 keeps it to this machine. Restart required; guarded because it decides who can reach the port.
The most rows one MCP tool call returns to an AI client.
de/settings.json::settings.mcp.port.help: The port the MCP server listens on; 0 leaves it off. Restart required; guarded because it opens or closes a listener.
de/settings.json::settings.mcp.principal: The principal (user id) local (stdio) MCP calls act for, beside the local role; that person's entitlements narrow the role. Until it is set those calls are refused. Guarded because it acts with that person's access for anyone who can start the local client.
de/settings.json::settings.mcp.render_ti: How long render_graph may take to draw one graph as a PNG before it is stopped.
de/settings.json::settings.mcp.role.help: The role local (stdio) MCP calls run as; until it is set those calls are refused. Guarded because it grants that role's access to anyone who can start the local client.
de/settings.json::settings.mcp.stats_max: The most rows a statistics tool (correlate, regress, forecast, and describe's quantiles and top values) reads to fit a model. Counts, means and group comparisons are computed by the engine over every row. A result that holds more says so.
de/settings.json::settings.mcp.tls.help: Whether the MCP server serves HTTPS. Restart required; guarded.
de/settings.json::settings.mcp.tls.label: MCP TLS
de/settings.json::settings.mcp.tools.hel: The tools listed to an MCP client whose address names none (tools=full or tools=sip on the address). full lists every tool; sip lists the tools for finding, describing, querying and reading metrics, plus one tool that adds the other groups when the client asks. de/settings.json::settings.sandbox.memor: The most memory one demo sandbox's engine may use. A query that needs more is refused.
de/settings.json::settings.sandbox.templ: How many demo templates the sandbox tier builds together after it starts; the rest wait their turn, and a demo a visitor opens is built next. More finish sooner on a larger machine; on a small one, building them all at once leaves it too busy to serve visitors. Takes effect at the next start.
de/settings.json::settings.security.mode: Standard, or high security, where data endpoints refuse any client that cannot decrypt results itself and the pgwire, Bolt and MCP listeners are not started. de/settings.json::settings.server.grpc_p: The port the gRPC server listens on. Restart required; guarded because clients and firewalls must follow a change.
de/settings.json::settings.server.hostna: The host name the deployment advertises to clients in the addresses it hands out. Restart required because servers started at boot carry it.

de/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.cha: How Provisa learns rows changed. ttl = refresh on the Cache TTL timer; probe = source-native freshness query, re-pull only on change; ttl_probe = probe after the TTL floor elapses; native/debezium/kafka = source push. de/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.con: per-instance: each instance its own copy

Only matters when Provisa runs as several instances behind a load balancer. Shared: a single copy in the shared store, refreshed by one instance at a time (a short lease with fencing), so every instance reads the same consistent snapshot. Pick this when instances must agree. Per-instance: each instance builds and refreshes its own copy. This is simpler and faster, but instances can briefly disagree (eventually consistent), so it is safe only for a deterministic view over a source that's stable within a refresh cycle. Per-instance needs each instance to have its own store (e.g. an embedded/in-process DuckDB). With a shared external store (Postgres, Trino + object store, a warehouse) every instance writes the same physical table, so use shared.

de/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.pre: Optional preflight check run after the view SQL and before landing. Define preflight(streams, ctx) and return a verdict: ctx.ok() to continue, ctx.abort(reason) to reject (error + poison downstream), or ctx.quarantine(reason) to hold without landing. streams is a dict keyed by input node: streams["schema.table"] yields that input's rows lazily, so you inspect an input without materializing it. A check inspects rows and does not transform them (put transforms in SQL or an external processor). A SQL-expressible check, such as if any(...)/all(...) over one input's rows, is pushed down to the engine as a count probe over that input, so it scales to a billion rows; anything else streams each input as Arrow batches and short-circuits. Call ctx.warn(reason) for a non-fatal advisory. It may import one module, provisa_services, to call Provisa's services (dq among them); such a check always streams and its verdict is the state at refresh time. Otherwise it must be deterministic, with no clock, randomness, other imports, or IO, and it is purity-checked when you save; a non-deterministic or unsafe check is rejected.

de/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.upd: Keeps every version. Each refresh appends what changed, keyed on the business key, so the view can be read as of any time.

The query is not re-run. The single input delivers the rows that changed (as a delta), and only those rows are merged into the stored table by primary key, so work per refresh scales with the size of the change. The cheapest option for large, slowly-changing data. It needs a primary key and applies only when: (1) there is exactly one input (no joins), (2) that input emits a delta, meaning it runs on a change/CDC signal, and (3) the view SQL is a plain column projection (no join, filter, GROUP BY, aggregate, DISTINCT, or computed column), so the input's delta maps 1:1 to this view's delta. If a refresh brings no delta (a full-snapshot input or a probe trigger), that refresh is a full recompute.

Current state, no history. Every refresh re-runs the whole query and replaces the stored table with the fresh result. Simplest and always correct, but work per refresh scales with the total size of the inputs.

Current state, no history. Every refresh re-runs the whole query, then merges the result into the stored table by primary key, updating matching rows in place and inserting new ones. Nothing is deleted and reinserted. The query still recomputes everything, so work scales with total input size.

de/tagCitations.json::tagCitations.revie: A citation on this tag needs review: its section changed or is gone.
de/tagControl.json::tagControl.noTags: No tags apply to this object type
de/tagControl.json::tagControl.piiAlsoTe: Mark '{{term}}', so every column that means it is covered, those to come too?
Also mark the {{count}} other column that means '{{term}}'?
Also mark the {{count}} other columns that mean '{{term}}'?
de/tagControl.json::tagControl.piiInheri: This column is PII because it means {{term}}.
de/tagControl.json::tagControl.reasonReq: A reason is required for this tag
de/tagsTab.json::tagsTab.appliesToDesc: Object types this tag may attach to
de/tagsTab.json::tagsTab.deleteConfirm: Delete tag "{{id}}"? Its assignments are removed as well.
de/tagsTab.json::tagsTab.derivedTagHelp: Derived from each object's own registration and never assigned
de/tagsTab.json::tagsTab.heading: Tags
de/tagsTab.json::tagsTab.idDesc: Unique identifier for the tag. Lowercase letters, digits, _ and - only.
de/tagsTab.json::tagsTab.noValues: No values yet. Add one before making an assignment.
de/tagsTab.json::tagsTab.outsideBody: The save kept these assignments. Take the tag off an object where it no longer belongs.
de/tagsTab.json::tagsTab.paramPolicyDesc: Whether an assignment names a value, as in entity:customer
de/tagsTab.json::tagsTab.purposeAdd: A tag that applies to several object types is one tag, so editing it in any of the scoped lists edits it in all of them.
de/tagsTab.json::tagsTab.purposeBody: A tag is one org-wide label with fixed meaning, applied to sources, tables, columns, relationships, or commands. Tags change behavior: technical keeps a column out of the Data Product export, entity turns a column's values into retrieval vocabulary, deprecated tells consumers to migrate off.
de/tagsTab.json::tagsTab.requiredDesc: Every object of the kinds in Applies to must carry this tag. One without it shows as missing in the tags report.
de/team.json::teamPage.attributes.help: Attributes a row rule can read for this member. What the organization records here wins over the same attribute from their identity provider.
de/team.json::teamPage.dangerHelp: Deleting removes every source, domain, table, role and invite in this organization, for everyone in it. Download the configuration first if you want to keep it.
de/team.json::teamPage.deleteWarning: This permanently destroys {{org}} and everything registered in it. It cannot be undone, and Provisa keeps no copy.
de/team.json::teamPage.emailDesc: Send the invitation to this address. Leave empty for a link you share yourself.
de/team.json::teamPage.envPolicyDesc: A private environment is deployed from production, so the invitee sees your real model. It is deleted once it has gone unused for the span below, and the invitee is confined to it.
de/team.json::teamPage.envPolicyPerVisit: A fresh environment of their own
de/team.json::teamPage.expiresDesc: The link stops admitting anyone after this many days. Revoke it below to close it sooner.
de/team.json::teamPage.inviteHelp: Generate an invite link, pick the role the invitee is granted, and share the link. Signing in with it makes them a member of your organization.
de/team.json::teamPage.inviteNoMail: This deployment does not send email, so nothing was sent to {{email}}. Share this link instead: {{url}}
de/team.json::teamPage.inviteNotSent: The invitation for {{email}} was created but could not be sent ({{reason}}). Share this link instead: {{url}}
de/team.json::teamPage.lastAdminHint: This is the only org admin. Promote someone else first.
de/team.json::teamPage.openLinkDesc: An open link admits unlimited people and stays usable until it expires or you revoke it. Leave it off for a single-use invitation.
de/team.json::teamPage.openLinkLabel: Anyone with the link may join
de/team.json::teamPage.roleDesc: The role the invitee receives on joining. Shape what each role can do in Security → Roles.
de/team.json::teamPage.selfRemoveHint: Leave the organization from your profile instead.
de/team.json::teamPage.subtitle: Invite people into your organization and choose the role each of them receives.
de/team.json::teamPage.title: Admin Dashboard - Team
de/testData.json::testData.noConfidentMa: Tagged pii, with no confident match in the profile: declare its fake.
de/testData.json::testData.noProposal: The profile proposes nothing for this column.
de/testData.json::testData.savedAsHint: Written from your choice above; edit it to set arguments by hand
de/testData.json::testData.stableHint: The same fake on every engine and in every region
de/testData.json::testData.stableNeeds: A stable {{name}}() declares its {{args}}, so it is the same everywhere
de/testData.json::testData.stableNever: {{name}}() cannot be stable: it is not computed the same way on every engine
de/testData.json::testData.stableNoArgum: A stable {{name}}() takes no arguments: clear them to make it stable
de/testData.json::testData.stableNoFake: Choose a fake first: only a fake can be stable
de/testData.json::testData.stableVersion: Pinned to definition version {{version}}: its values stay the same until its fake changes
de/testData.json::testData.unmatchedPii: Tagged pii with no confident match, left for you: {{columns}}.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.affirmation.sum: An asset manager matches each of today's trades across its order system, its execution system, the broker and the custodian. Each break shows the time left to the cutoff and what a failed settlement would cost, and the trades that matched are affirmed.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.agentdata.summa: Can an AI agent be given a retailer's order data and held to what its user may see? The MCP explorer shows the agent as a support agent and as an analyst: different rows and columns, emails masked, and the governed SQL behind each answer.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.agentdata.title: Give an agent your data
de/tour.json::tour.demos.agriculture.sum: Does weather explain the losses in a crop insurer's portfolio? Its own farms, policies and claims, joined by county and crop year to the USDA's losses by cause, NOAA's weather and NASS's yields, answer it in SQL, GraphQL and REST.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.audit.summary: Do a nonprofit client's recorded federal awards match what the government's records show paying it? An audit firm's client schedules, joined to Single Audit filings and USAspending obligations, answer it.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.audit.title: Single Audit readiness
de/tour.json::tour.demos.banking.summary: A bank's end-of-day totals, built at each close straight from a ledger that is never copied to the warehouse, read as reported and as restated, with the same answer over GraphQL, SQL and an agent.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.banking.title: EOD reporting without copying the ledger
de/tour.json::tour.demos.banksecrecy.sum: A bank reads the Bank Secrecy Act's cash reporting rule from its official public address, finds its terms and grounds them on its own tables, then asks by concept which cash needs a currency transaction report and who is structuring just under $10,000. The bank and its customers are made up; the regulation is real.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.banksecrecy.tit: Cash reports read from the Bank Secrecy Act
de/tour.json::tour.demos.churn.summary: Which customers are about to cancel? Their governed, masked features are read into pandas in the browser, and a scikit-learn model is trained on them in the notebook that ships with the demo.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.churn.title: Predict customer churn
de/tour.json::tour.demos.churnprod.summa: The churn demo's scikit-learn model in production. Its Python package is a source, and its function is a table that scores every customer in a join, with masks and row rules applied to what it returns.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.churnprod.title: Churn risk in production
de/tour.json::tour.demos.cloudpolicy.sum: A security policy reviewed across Azure, AWS and Google Cloud. The cloud inventory, the ServiceNow incidents and the policy itself, read from its web page by code, are one model, and a daily trigger keeps the review's history.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.customer360.sum: Salesforce, ServiceNow, Jira and Stripe joined through a customer master to find the renewals at risk, then the master checked against each system's own evidence, which finds the account it missed.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.dataroom.summar: A retailer selling itself gives each bidder's clean team governed, time-limited access to its own systems with no exports: aggregates, profiles and masked samples, and no customer identity leaves the room.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.dataroom.title: Data room for a sale
de/tour.json::tour.demos.datavault.summa: A data vault declared over an order system and a CRM. The engine builds and refreshes its hubs, links and satellites as rows arrive, personal data is masked in the satellites, and one point-in-time query shows what was known about a customer, from which source, and when.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.datavault.title: Data vault
de/tour.json::tour.demos.files.summary: A city's open-data files read in place as one catalog: which neighborhoods have the most complaints near active construction?
de/tour.json::tour.demos.files.title: Instant data lake
de/tour.json::tour.demos.groupexposure.s: Which corporate groups is a bank over its large-exposure limit to? Its loan book, joined by each borrower's owner's LEI to Wikidata's chains of parent organizations over SPARQL, rolls each borrower up to its group. The bank and its borrowers are fictional; the groups are real.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.hasuramigration: A Hasura v2 storefront imported in one step, its queries reshaped once, then joined to the sales team's Salesforce accounts under the same rules.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.insider.summary: A bank checks its outbound mail against the watch list of deals in discussion, and for customer data. Everything is ranked in one review queue that a first-level reviewer works through without ever seeing the list.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.insider.title: Insider review
de/tour.json::tour.demos.insurance.summa: Where is a property insurer's exposure concentrated against hazard risk? Its own policies, joined by county to FEMA, wildfire and storm data, answer it in SQL, GraphQL and REST.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.insurance.title: Property exposure and hazard risk
de/tour.json::tour.demos.opioids.summary: Which counties have the most overdose deaths for the treatment their opioid settlement money pays for? A fund's allocations, joined by county to CDC, Census and federal spending data, answer a local government's question.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.opioids.title: Opioid settlement funds and overdose deaths
de/tour.json::tour.demos.pharma.summary: Which of a hospital pharmacy's products face shortage or recall risk? Its formulary and stock, joined to FDA's shortages and recalls and Medicaid's prescriptions, answer it in SQL, GraphQL and REST.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.pharma.title: Drug shortage and recall risk
de/tour.json::tour.demos.profiling.summa: An acquired company's customers and orders, profiled by the built-in Data Profiler: nulls, ranges, formats, plausible types and duplicates, landed as governed tables and read in SQL, GraphQL and REST.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.profiling.title: What is actually in this data?
de/tour.json::tour.demos.provisioning.su: How do downstream teams get big datasets as soon as they're ready? Feeds land from Kafka, datasets refresh as they land, and each team is told on Kafka and pulls over Arrow Flight as of that moment.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.quality.summary: A chain of shops' sales feed, refined from bronze to silver and gold by checked materialized views. Landing a batch is all it takes, and a batch that fails a check never reaches silver.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.quality.title: Data you can trust
de/tour.json::tour.demos.reproduce.summa: A regulator's two questions about a bank's exposure report: where a figure came from, and what the report said when it was filed, untouched by a correction since. Lineage, as-of replay and the audit log answer both.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.reproduce.title: Reproduce a report
de/tour.json::tour.demos.retail.summary: A retail group with an EU and a US subsidiary run as one business under GDPR: EU data stays in the EU, group reporting reads it pseudonymised, and access, erasure, insider review and audit are each one query.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.retail.title: A Tale of Two Regions
de/tour.json::tour.demos.reviews.summary: An electronics shop's catalog, reviews and purchases in MongoDB, Elasticsearch and Neo4j, joined on the product: which products do reviews say the battery dies on, and what else did their buyers buy?
de/tour.json::tour.demos.reviews.title: Product reviews
de/tour.json::tour.demos.sonnets.summary: The 154 sonnets embedded, searched by meaning and grown into a graph: the themes they share and the lines where Shakespeare echoes himself.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.sonnets.title: Shakespeare's sonnets
de/tour.json::tour.demos.storefront.summ: An app's order-history screen and a BI dashboard read one model of PostgreSQL, MongoDB and a REST service, under the same relationships and rules.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.streaming.summa: A coffee shop's orders arrive live on Kafka and are joined to its catalog. A view of the busiest regions over the last five minutes refreshes with every batch, answers in SQL, GraphQL and REST, can be cached, and can be watched with a subscription.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.streaming.title: Live order stream
de/tour.json::tour.demos.testdata.summar: A shop's production database in three environments: the real rows in prod, production's rows with every sensitive column faked in pre-prod, and generated rows with nothing real in dev.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.testdata.title: Test data
de/tour.json::tour.demos.vulnerabilities: Which exploited vulnerabilities are in a software company's code, and how far past CISA's due date are they? Its Dependabot alerts, joined by CVE to the NVD and CISA's catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, answer it.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.weblogs.summary: Which pages of a web shop are slow, and which SQL makes them slow? See the shop's sources, the tables they become, the join between its two logs, and the answer in SQL and over REST.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.weblogs.title: The web shop's logs
de/tour.json::tour.demos.worldcup.summar: Wikipedia's and Kaggle's World Cup data disagree on country names. A short Python function matches every name with an LLM, and the public sources become one governed graph.
de/tour.json::tour.demos.worldcup.title: World Cup, one graph
de/tour.json::tour.menu.intro: One model for your data, metadata and processing, kept in sync and reused everywhere. Each topic is a short tour of its own, and Done brings you back here. The compass in the toolbar reopens this menu anytime.
de/tour.json::tour.menu.title: Deep Dives
de/tour.json::tour.nav.anyTime: You can restart the tour or open the Deep Dives any time from the tour button.
de/tour.json::tour.status.stuck: This step is taking longer than expected. The page may still be loading.
de/tour.json::tour.status.waiting: Waiting for this page to finish loading…
de/tour.json::tour.steps.affirmationAffi: A command affirmed every allocation that matched in all four systems and logged each one at the desk's time. It ran once, when the demo was built.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.affirmationBrok: The brokers' confirmations, as the matching platform delivers them: each carries the allocation's reference, the broker's price, commission and net amount, and the account the broker will deliver to.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.affirmationCust: The settlement instructions Larkspur sent its custodian: what each fund receives or delivers, against what cash, on what day. A trade the custodian was never told about fails as surely as a wrong one.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.affirmationExpl: The statement the agent sent, next to the one Provisa ran for the role. The agent read the same governed views and tables you just did.
The explorer's agent answers live over Provisa's MCP server, as the header's role, and you can watch each query it runs.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.affirmationFeed: This relationship joins each allocation's records from the four systems to trade_match and passes them as its parameters: one call for each allocation. Querying the join runs the match.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.affirmationMatc: trade_match is a table like any other: its columns are what the function returns, and its parameters are the four systems' fields. A leg that has not arrived is passed as absent, and the function names that as a break of its own.
A Python package registered as a source. Its trade_match function takes one allocation's four records and returns a row for each break it finds, naming the break and what differs, or one matched row.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.affirmationPoll: Polly reads the break queue and names the break with the least time to its cutoff. Its answer was made when the demo was built, and is shown as stored.
Ask Polly: what is most urgent?
Polly names the break whose failed settlement would cost most a day. Its answer was made when the demo was built, and is shown as stored.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.affirmationQueu: Each break, with the minutes left before its market's affirmation cutoff and what a failed settlement would accrue a day there. The European breaks have under an hour; the US ones have until 9 pm in New York.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.affirmationReca: Four systems read live, matched by a Python function registered as a table, every break named with its time to cutoff and its cost, and the matched trades affirmed by a command. Ask the desk's own questions in Explore next.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.affirmationScen: Larkspur Asset Management traded ten orders today. Each trade lives in four systems that never see one another: this order management system with its allocations to the funds, the execution system's fills, the broker's confirmation and the custodian's settlement instruction. Which trades will not affirm before the cutoff, why, and what would a failed settlement cost?
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agentdataAnalys: Asked as the analyst, every region comes back, there is no email column at all, and the revenue view is among its tables. Different tables, rows and columns, from the same agent and the same server.
Next switches the header to the BI analyst. The agent is the same; the role is different.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agentdataConnec: This is the server the explorer's agent used. Paste this config into Claude Desktop, or point any MCP client at the URL, and your own agent gets the same governed tools, held to the same rules.
Your own agent, the same server
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agentdataCustom: The customers table carries the rules. A West support agent reads only the West's customers and their orders, with email addresses masked and no prices. The BI analyst reads every region and what the orders came to, but no email address at all.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agentdataExplai: Opening the agent's run_sql call shows the statement it sent, then the statement that ran for its role. Provisa added the West row filter and the email mask. The agent wrote neither, and is never told about them.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agentdataOutOfR: Asked what each customer's orders came to, the agent finds no prices among the tables its role can read, and says so. It cannot reach around the role, because the same rules hold on every tool call.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agentdataScenar: A retailer wants an AI agent on its order data, held to what the person it acts for may see. The agent reaches the data over Provisa's MCP server. The MCP explorer, coming up, shows exactly what such an outside agent sees. Polly, by contrast, is the assistant for working in Provisa itself. This is the retailer's order database, read live.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agentdataSuppor: The agent acts as the role in the header, now the West support agent, so every tool call it makes runs as that role. The agent finds the tables, writes SQL and runs it through MCP tools, shown as they run. Only the West's customers come back, and their email addresses arrive masked, which is all the role is served.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureAnsw: The view losses_and_weather sets each county's season beside the portfolio's results, and is kept stored. Read by crop year, 2012, the driest and hottest season, is the year the portfolio lost money, mostly to drought and heat, as the whole market did; the wet years of 2010 and 2013 cost less.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureClai: Each indemnity the insurer paid, with the farm, the crop year, the cause of loss, the month and the amount.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureDryS: The same view in GraphQL, the seasons with the least rain first. They are the ones with the highest loss ratios and the lowest yields.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureGovd: The government data comes from AskAmerica.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureJoin: The portfolio and the public tables share the county's FIPS code, and these relationships join them. The answer's view matches them by county and crop year.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureMark: The USDA Risk Management Agency publishes every county's crop insurance experience by crop, cause of loss and month: the premium the market earned and the indemnities it paid for drought, heat, excess moisture, hail and the rest. This demo covers the crop years 2010 to 2017.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureNote: The demo's notebook runs in your browser. It reads every county season into pandas as the analyst, correlates the loss ratio with the season's rain, its days above 32 °C and the share of the market's losses down to drought and heat, fits a regression on them and plots it.
How much does the weather explain?
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureReca: You saw the insurer's own data matched by county and crop year to public losses, weather and yields, all in one governed model. One view answers whether the weather explains the losses, in SQL, GraphQL and REST. The notebook measures it. The weather explains 54% of the variation in loss ratio, and across today's book a 2012-like season has an expected loss ratio of 1.75.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureRest: The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped by crop year and summed on the server. Any client that speaks HTTP gets the answer without writing SQL.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureScen: A crop insurer wants to know whether weather explains the losses in its portfolio. Its own farms, policies and claims are in its database; the weather of every US county, and the whole market's crop insurance losses by cause, are public, in NOAA's and the USDA's data. The tour shows Provisa joining the two by county and crop year, and answering the question in SQL, GraphQL and over REST.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureTerm: The ontology names what a crop underwriter asks about: loss ratio, cause of loss, actual production history, coverage level, liability and the growing season. Here, the loss ratio is indemnities divided by premium. Above 1, the year lost money.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureWeat: NOAA's daily maximum temperature and precipitation for each county, the mean of its reporting stations, over the growing season, May to August, when rain and heat decide the yield.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureWors: The county seasons with the highest loss ratios, beside their rain, their days above 32 °C, the share of the market's losses the USDA puts down to drought and heat, and the corn yield NASS recorded.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditAnswer.des: The view readiness answers the same question for every client at once, and is kept stored. It sets each schedule line beside its award records and the public record of the program, and lists the items each readiness memo needs.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditAsTeam.des: Run as the Maine engagement team, the same view returns only the Maine team's three clients. Row rules on each table and on the view keep every team to its own engagements. The partner sees them all.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditCounty.des: What USAspending recorded obligating in each client's county in federal fiscal 2023, by program, counted where the work is done. It shows whether a program the client schedules is paying out in its county at all.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditCountyJoin: Each client's county code joins it to USAspending's county obligations, and its Assistance Listings join its schedule to the public filings of the same program in its state.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditExample.de: The readiness memo's items as a GraphQL query, for the firm's own engagement tools.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditFiled.desc: Every award line the three states' auditees filed for 2023, beside what USAspending recorded obligating to them under the same program that year. An unmatched line is not by itself a gap. A passed-through line reached the auditee through a state agency, so no federal award names it and none is expected to match; and an award obligated in an earlier year shows no obligation in the audit year. The unmatched lines are kept, not hidden.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditFiled.titl: The same match, on public filings
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditGovdata.de: The government data comes from AskAmerica: every award line of the 2023 Single Audits filed with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse in Vermont, New Hampshire and Maine, each set beside what USAspending obligated to the same recipient under the same program, and USAspending's obligations by county and program.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditLineage.de: The lineage traces each column of the answer back through the view to the firm's tables and the public data, so a reviewer can see where every figure in the memo came from.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditNotices.de: The federal award records each client holds for its direct awards: one row for each obligation, the federal fiscal year it was made in and the amount. A multi-year award may have been obligated before the year it was spent.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditPollyDiffe: Polly sets the schedule beside the award records and lists every award where the two do not agree, with the query behind its answer.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditPollyKinds: A timing difference is an award obligated in an earlier year and spent this year, which needs only an explanation. A missing award is a direct line with no federal record behind it, which needs a correction. Polly sorts the differences into the two kinds.
Last, the memo: each item the client has to explain or correct before fieldwork starts, from the timing differences to the award its schedule leaves out.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditPollyRecor: Next, the government's side: what the client's federal award records show obligated to it in federal fiscal 2023. One of the obligations is for a program the schedule does not list.
What the records show paying it
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditPollySched: The analyst starts with what the client records. Polly lists the awards on its 2023 schedule and shows the SQL it ran. Its answer was generated when the demo was built and is stored with it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditPublic.des: The same match, run on the public filings of the three states. These are the programs whose direct award lines most often have no USAspending obligation in the audit year. They are shown as they are, and they show why an unmatched line is a question for the auditor rather than an error.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditRecap.desc: The firm's own client records and the government's public filings and obligations, joined in one governed model. One stored view answers the partner's question for every client. Each team reads only its own clients, and every query is recorded.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditRecordedAs: This relationship joins each schedule line to its award records by the firm's award reference. A line with no record behind it, and a record with no line, are what the auditor looks for.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditRequest.de: The partner asks the analyst to get Brindlewood Community Health ready for fieldwork. This is its draft schedule: five federal programs, three of them direct awards. Next, the analyst works through the request with Polly.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditRest.descr: The view is also a REST endpoint, grouped by finding and summed on the server, so a workpaper spreadsheet can read it over HTTP.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditRest.title: The same answer over REST
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditScenario.d: An audit firm audits nine nonprofits that spend federal grants. Before fieldwork, the partner asks whether each client's recorded federal awards match what the government's records show paying it. The clients' schedules and award records are in the firm's own database; the Single Audit filings and federal obligations are public. The clients and their figures are made up; the programs, counties and public data are real.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditSchedule.d: Each client's draft Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards for 2023: one line for each award, with its Assistance Listing, whether it came direct from a federal agency or through a state agency, and what the client says it spent.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.auditTerms.desc: The ontology explains the terms of a Single Audit: the schedule, the Assistance Listing, the pass-through entity, the obligation, a timing difference, a missing award and the readiness memo.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingAgent.de: An agent connected over MCP reads the same model. Polly answers this question from the same end-of-day totals the dashboard and BI read, so it names the same branch.
The dashboard is what operations sees. The rest of the tour is back as the administrator, and each statement that follows names the role it runs as.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingAsOpsSql: The explorer now runs as operations.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingChange.d: Suppose volumes outgrow the ledger's compute. Set this table's region to warehouse and its replicate setting to Always, and the ledger is replicated into the warehouse. That is a two-line placement change, and every query, dashboard, BI view and agent answers as before. Built by hand, the same move means new pipelines, a backfill, rewritten aggregation and versioning, repointed reports and a second set of access rules. Then come reconciliation testing, audit and lineage checks, architecture and security review, and a change board. Here the change is a two-line reviewed diff, and that diff is what testing, audit and architecture review.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingChange.t: Changing your mind costs two lines
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingCloses.d: The end-of-day totals are a view materialized in the warehouse on the bank's calendar, which closes at 18:00 London time. The view is one GROUP BY over the ledger's one table, so its build runs whole at the ledger and only the grouped rows come back. It inherits the ledger's versions and needs no history settings of its own. Each day was recorded at its own close. 1 and 2 October were recorded again later, when their restatements arrived.
This works when the ledger's side has the compute to run the end-of-day GROUP BY. Replicating is not free for it either. Every changed row has to be found, read in full and shipped, and aggregating in place is often lighter. With high volumes, reports that read totals and an occasional drill-down, keeping the ledger home tends to win. The declaration lets you choose either way.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingDashboar: This query runs as operations, who drill into postings under the ledger's own rules. They see no posting to a staff account, and every counterparty is withheld. London's totals for 1 October, each with the postings behind it nested inside. One request reads the totals from the warehouse and the postings from the ledger, joined along the relationship you just saw.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingDay.desc: This SQL runs as the bank's reporting analysts. They read the end-of-day totals and the five ledger columns the totals are built from: business date, branch, product, currency and amount. They never see an account, a counterparty or a holder. 1 October as it stands now. For each branch, product and currency you see what came in, what went out and the net. A BI tool connected over pgwire runs this same SQL.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingJoin.des: Each total carries one key made of its day, branch, product and currency. This relationship follows that key to the postings that carry it, read live from the ledger. The drill-down needs no copy either.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingJoin.tit: From a total to its postings
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingLedger.d: The transaction table is homed in the ledger region and never replicated. No copy of a posting ever lands in the warehouse, and every query over the table runs in the ledger. The end-of-day totals and the drill-downs come off the warehouse's bill, for modest compute in the ledger. Only the totals reach the warehouse, plus the postings a drill-down shows, in passing.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingPostings: London's corporate GBP postings for 1 October, read live from the ledger. The recalled payment appears as its latest version, reversed. Its counterparty is withheld, like every other, and a posting to a staff account would not appear. The ledger's rules apply to the drill-down wherever it is read from.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingRecap.de: The end-of-day totals were computed at the ledger, and the warehouse paid only for what it keeps. The warehouse holds totals and never postings, so there is no second copy of the ledger to govern. The dashboard, BI and the agent read one declared relationship and gave the same numbers. If keeping the ledger home turns out wrong, a two-line placement change moves it while nothing that reads it changes.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingReported: The corporate totals for 1 and 2 October, as reported at 1 October's close. The view's as_recorded argument reads it as it had been recorded then, and a BI tool on pgwire does the same with SET provisa.as_recorded. London's GBP total still carries the payment that was later reversed. 2 October had not closed yet, so it has no figures.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingRestated: The same SQL with as_recorded at 12 October's close, the last of the thirty days. London's 1 October total no longer carries the reversed payment, and Edinburgh's 2 October USD total now includes the late trade. The versions reported at each close are kept beside the restated ones, and recorded_at shows when each was recorded.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingScenario: A bank reports its totals at every business day's 18:00 close, and restates a past day when a correction arrives later. The usual way first copies the ledger into the warehouse, and this demo does not. As you go, watch what the reporting costs to compute, how much data the warehouse holds and must govern, whether the dashboard, BI and an agent give the same answer, and what it costs to change the decision later.
End-of-day reporting, ledger left in place
de/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingVersions: The ledger never changes a posting. A correction is a new row with the same transaction id, and it keeps the business date. Three mappings tell Provisa so. The business key is transaction_id, the valid time is business_date and the recorded time is updated_at. Anything built on the table can then be read as of a day, or as it was recorded at a time.
A correction is a new row
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyAggr: 31 CFR 1010.313 is where multiple transactions and on behalf of come from: cash by or on behalf of one person, over $10,000 in one business day, is treated as a single transaction, and every branch is one institution. Night deposits count on the next business day.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyBusi: The regulation's business day is the day a bank posts a transaction to the customer's account. The bank's business_day column holds exactly that, so the term holds the column itself.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyCash: Every cash deposit and withdrawal at a teller's window: the account, the branch, the teller, the time, and the business day it posted to. Cash taken after the 17:00 cutoff posts to the next business day.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyComp: The compliance officer runs the same question and sees account numbers and tax ids in full, as the report needs them. Dana Whitmore's total includes cash brought in on her behalf by someone else.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyDefi: The rule's words are defined in 31 CFR 1010.100: person, business day, financial institution, structuring. Each definition is its own passage, so each term is offered with the paragraph that defines it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyExam: The reports due, as an API call. Each surface reads the same governed view, with the same masks for the same role.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyFind: Typing the regulation's address and starting a scan

Find terms reads a document from its address. Here it is 31 CFR 1010.311 on eCFR's official API. A scan asks the AI model about every passage and takes minutes, so the tour stopped this one. The same scan ran when the demo was built.
Read the law from its public address
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyGrou: Transaction in currency is the regulation's term. The bank's cash transaction is a kind of it, so the term reaches the cash_transactions table. Person reaches customers the same way, and a financial institution reaches the bank's branches.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyLibr: The demo's build kept each scanned document in the reference library, so the regulation stays with the model as a governed reference: Polly and the org's agents cite its passages when they answer.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyOnBe: Each transaction names who stood at the window and whose cash it is. When an employee or a relative brings cash in, it counts toward the account holder's total, which is how the law counts it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyPoll: Compliance asks Polly in plain words: which cash needs a currency transaction report? Polly finds the governed view the concept reaches and answers from it, so it names the same people the SQL and the GraphQL returned. Nobody had to know the view's name.

A customer keeps depositing cash just under $10,000. What must the bank do? Searching the law's passages for those words misses the answer. Polly walks the glossary instead: deposits under threshold, to structuring, to suspicious activity report, and reaches 31 CFR 1010.314 and 31 CFR 1020.320, the passages that say.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyReca: The law was read from its public address, its terms were found and grounded on the bank's tables, and the bank asked by concept. The currency transaction report reaches the data through its multiple transactions, and each role saw what it may see.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyRule: The scan done ahead: each candidate term with the passage it comes from. A financial institution reports each transaction in currency of more than $10,000. Terms the glossary already holds are offered as merges.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyScen: A community bank must report cash over $10,000 under the Bank Secrecy Act. This demo reads the rule itself from its public address, finds the terms it uses, grounds them on the bank's data, and then asks by concept: which cash needs a currency transaction report, and who is structuring? It starts with the bank's core system, read live where it is.
A bank reads a US law
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyStru: Deposits just under $10,000, three or more times, across branches and days. None of them needed a report on its own. Victor Hale went to three branches in a week, and Marcus Reed's two deposits on one day needed a report together. Only compliance sees this view.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.banksecrecyTell: Asked by concept: cash in, or cash out, of more than $10,000 by or on behalf of one person on one business day, the multiple transactions counted as one across accounts and branches. A teller sees the reports due, with account numbers and tax ids masked.
Which cash needs a report? As a teller
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnAnalyst.de: Next, the role picker switches to analyst, the role the data scientist reads with, so every surface after this runs as the analyst.
Each customer's plan, region, tenure and the day they cancelled, if they have. Their email address is masked for the analyst role, arriving as *** and its domain.
Next, the role picker switches back to All.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnFeatures.d: One row a customer, with plan, tenure, sign-ins a month, tickets in the year, and whether they cancelled. A materialized view, built through the governed pipeline. The email addresses are masked, as the analyst is served them.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnFeatures.t: The features the model learns from
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnGraphql.de: The demo's example query reads the same view as the analyst, with the same mask.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnNotebook.d: The demo's notebook, run in the Notebook tab, reads the features into pandas as the analyst, trains a scikit-learn model on them and lists the customers most at risk. Python runs in your browser, and the email addresses are still masked.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnNotebook.t: A model, trained in your browser
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnRecap.desc: Governed data went straight into a data scientist's notebook, with the analyst's mask applied on the way in and a model trained without the data leaving the browser. In a desktop Jupyter the same code reads large pulls over Arrow Flight. The churnprod demo puts this model in production.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnScenario.d: A subscription business wants to know which customers are about to cancel. Its customers and a year of their monthly usage are in its own database, and a data scientist trains a model on them in the browser.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnUsage.desc: Twelve months of each customer's sign-ins and support tickets, joined to the customer they belong to.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodAnalys: The analyst reads the same list, as the churn demo's analyst reads its features.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodAtRisk: Every current customer, scored by the model and ranked by risk, with the reasons that raise each score most. It is one SQL statement over a view, and the model is called inside it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodColumn: churn_risk is a table because its docstring says @table. Its columns are the fields of the RiskRow it returns. Its parameters are its arguments, the customer and each feature the model was trained on.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodJoin.d: This relationship joins each customer to the model's score, so a join over customers scores every one of them.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodJoin.t: The join that feeds the model
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodMasked: The scores are the same. The email addresses are masked, because the analyst's mask applies to the list as it applies to the customers' table.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodNode.d: Here is the same model in JavaScript. Its fitted coefficients were exported from Python, and it is registered as a Node source beside the Python one. Each customer gets the same score from both.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodPackag: The model's package is a source. It carries the fitted model and a lockfile that pins scikit-learn.
A data scientist's model went to production with no service of its own to run. Its package is pinned. A join feeds its function, which reads as a table, and the masks and row rules every table has govern what it returns. SQL, GraphQL and every other way in read it the same way.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodRegion: The EU account team looks after the customers billed in the EU.
Now as the EU account team
Only EU customers are listed. The row rule sits on churn_risk itself, and a rule on a code table applies to the rows its code returns.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodScenar: The churn demo's data scientist trained a scikit-learn model on the customers' usage to find who is about to cancel. Here that model goes to production. It ships as a Python package, and it scores every customer you may see, under the same rules as any table.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyAppT: The payments team reads its own resources and incidents only.
The same statement returns only the payments team's disks. The row rules sit on the inventory and the incidents, and every view built on them applies them.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyAudi: The auditor reads every account in every cloud.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyCite: Each incident cites a policy section. This relationship joins it to the clause it cites, so an incident filed under the wrong section shows up.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyDash: Superset reads the same views through Provisa's Postgres protocol. Here is its compliance dashboard, with the violations by control.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyInci: The second source is the security team's ServiceNow incidents. Each one names the disk it is about as its configuration item, and it cites the policy section it is filed under. An exception is an incident in the Policy exception category.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyMode: Each disk names the machine it is attached to. This relationship joins disks to machines in Azure, AWS and Google Cloud alike.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyOpen: Here is every disk the review flags, for every team.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyPoli: Here is every control of the policy, read from its HTML with its heading, its clause and the day it took effect. Section 4.2 is the disk-encryption control under review.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyPoll: An exception lasts 90 days under section 4.3. Polly finds the disks it still covers.
The policy has controls that no check enforces. Polly compares the policy with the checks the team runs, and it can draft a view for a steward to add.
Polly reads the same governed model you do. It names the disks without a customer-managed key and the section that requires one.
Ask Polly who breaks the control
Some incidents cite a section other than the control they are about, and one cites a section the policy withdrew.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyRead: The policy itself is a web page. This Python package ships with the page and reads it into a row for each control. Its function is a table, so the policy joins the rest of the model.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyReca: You reviewed one policy across three clouds from what was already recorded. The policy is a table, read by code from its own page, and each incident joins the clause it cites. A daily trigger keeps the history, and each role reads only what its rules allow, in SQL, in Polly and in Superset.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyRevi: The daily review classifies each attached disk by the policy's rules. A disk without a customer-managed key may be covered by an exception in date. If it is not, its incident is within its deadline or past it, closed with the disk still not compliant, or never filed.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyScen: Your security policy says every disk attached to a virtual machine uses a customer-managed key. You lead security, and you review that across Azure, AWS and Google Cloud from what is already recorded. The first source is the cloud inventory. It lists every machine and disk in the three clouds, with the key each disk is encrypted with.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicySear: A search by meaning finds the control about disk encryption even when your words differ from the clause's.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyTren: The history the trigger keeps shows the violations day by day. Disks drop out as their incidents are fixed, and a new violation shows up the day it appears.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyTrig: Each morning a scheduled trigger runs the review and writes the day's rows to the review history. It writes through the same governed pipeline as any statement, under its role's write grant.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyViol: Section 4.2 is written as a view. It lists every attached disk whose key the cloud manages, beside the machine the disk is on.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Answ: renewal_risk_hub answers the question: each account whose renewal closes this quarter, with the open P1 incidents, blocked fixes and overdue invoices of the records the hub links to it. Seven accounts. This quarter and overdue are measured from the hub's last sync.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Corr: renewal_risk_checked asks again through the hub with its findings applied. Larkspur Analytics appears: its last invoice is overdue, but the hub linked it to Larkspur Labs' Stripe customer, so the first answer missed it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Cros: xref is the crosswalk: each row is one system's id for a customer and the master it belongs to, with who linked it and when: the initial load, a steward, the support desk or a bulk import.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Find: hub_findings lists every disagreement: two wrong merges (the bulk import swapped the Larkspur Stripe customers), duplicate customers, coverage gaps (records in no master) and stale links (to records a system no longer holds). Crosswalk, master and findings are one cascade of materialized views.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Fixe: FIXED_BY follows a ServiceNow incident's correlation id to the Jira bug that fixes it: the link the two teams already keep.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Grap: The path behind each open P1, as a graph: a Salesforce account, its crosswalk row, its master customer, the master's ServiceNow company, the P1 incidents it raised and the Jira bug fixing each. Every hop goes through the hub.
The same view as a GraphQL query, with the master customer each account belongs to. Every table and view is a GraphQL field, governed the same way.
hub is Halyard's customer master, a Postgres database read live. It holds one master customer for each real customer, and a crosswalk from each master to its id in every system. It is the system of record for who is who.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Jira: A Jira table is a form: one project and issue type, here the ENG project's bugs. Its customer column reads the custom field customfield_10050, the customer's name as the support engineer typed it, so one customer can be spelled several ways.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Line: The answer's lineage: each column traced back through renewal_risk_hub to the fields it reads in Salesforce's opportunities and accounts, the hub's crosswalk, ServiceNow's incidents, Jira's bugs and Stripe's invoices.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Prod: Account Health is the data product: the checked answer, the golden customer record, the findings and the match rate, with its purpose, usage and limitations stated.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Reca: Four SaaS systems with no shared id, joined through a customer master; the question answered in SQL, GraphQL and Cypher; then checked: rules re-derived every link from evidence and found the wrong merge and the account it hid. Look around on your own from the SQL page.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Rule: crosswalk matches each system record to a Salesforce account by a rule it names: the website or email domain, else the normalised name. The two Larkspur Stripe customers match by email domain, one to Larkspur Analytics and one to Larkspur Labs. master builds the golden record; its id is a hash of the anchor account, so a rebuild never renumbers it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Scen: Halyard Software sells to businesses, and each customer lives in four systems: Salesforce holds its account and renewals, ServiceNow its incidents, Jira engineering's bugs and Stripe its invoices. The question: which accounts renewing this quarter have open P1 incidents, blocked fixes or overdue invoices? On the way: SaaS sources, a customer master read live, relationships, lineage, materialized views, data-quality findings and a data product.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Spok: IS_BILLED_AS relates a crosswalk row to the Stripe customer it names. Each system relates to the hub this way, not to the other systems, so a fifth system is one more relationship, not four.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Syst: stripe is Halyard's Stripe account, read through Stripe's published API. Like Salesforce, ServiceNow and Jira, it knows a customer only by its own id: cus_… here, 001… in Salesforce, a company sys_id in ServiceNow, a typed name in Jira's Customer field. No id is shared.
Each system has its own ids
de/tour.json::tour.steps.customer360Trus: The answer is only as good as the hub's links. hub_match_rate re-derives each link from the evidence in the systems' own records and shows, month by month, the share it confirms. It fell after the bulk import.
How far can you trust that answer?
Orders, revenue and the average order of each segment, by year, from the orders and the customers' segments.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomAudit.d: Every statement is audited: who ran it, as which role, the tables it read, whether it was answered and how many rows it returned. Here are the statements you just ran as bidder A and bidder B.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomBidderB: Bidder B's clean team holds its own role, bidder_b, granted the same room and ending on the same date. Neither bidder sees what the other asks.
Customers who first ordered in the first quarter of 2023, and how many still ordered in each quarter after, with what they spent.
How many customers each segment and region has, and how many ordered in the last twelve months.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomCrm.des: The sales team's Salesforce holds each business customer's account and its deals. Its rows are landed once into the room and read from there, so the bidders' questions never reach Salesforce.
The Users page lists each grant with its end date and its last use. After the deal date the grants are gone, removed by the schedule and recorded in the org's trail, and nothing more leaves the room.
Access ends on the deal date
de/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomGrant.d: Each analyst's grant of bidder_a ends on the deal date. From that moment the role is no longer theirs, on every request however it arrives. An account has no end date of its own; the grant's end ends the access.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomGrant.t: A grant that ends on the deal date
de/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomIntro.d: Northfield Supply is selling itself, and each prospective buyer's clean team needs to see the business before it bids. Instead of exporting extracts into a data room, the seller connects Provisa to its own systems and gives each bidder governed access that ends on the deal date. Nothing is copied out, and no customer identity leaves the room. This is the order and finance system, a Postgres database read in place, with 2,400 customers, their orders since 2023 and the invoice of each.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomIntro.t: A data room with no exports
