On the seller's Users page, bidder A's two analysts are added as local accounts, each bound to the bidder_a role. They sign in to the seller's Provisa over HTTPS. A self-hosted seller exposes only HTTPS, through its own TLS edge (an ingress or reverse proxy with a public certificate), while the stores, the engine and the database protocols stay private; on hosted Provisa the org's own address already serves it. Nothing in this demo opens a port.
Setting up the room: invite the analysts
de/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomPipelin: The CRM's deals by industry and stage, with their value and their value weighted by the chance each closes. The businesses' and the deals' names stay in the CRM.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomProfile: These statements run as bidder_a, exactly as the analysts' do. Each column of the invoices table as the profiler found it, with its rows, nulls, distinct values and range. A bidder learns how complete the records are without reading one of them. Here, some invoices have never been paid.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomQuality: Each check of the seller's records and how many rows fail it: customers with no email, phone numbers that are not ten digits, invoices never paid.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomRecap.d: A data room with no exports. The seller's own systems are read in place and shown to each bidder as aggregates, profiles, quality scores, masked samples and records without identities. No customer identity leaves the room. Each bidder holds a role of its own, granted until the deal date, and every statement is audited.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomRefused: Bidder A asks for the customers' names. Provisa refuses, because no customer name is granted to bidder_a, and neither are the CRM's business and deal names. Had the analyst named bidder B's role, which they do not hold, the request would be refused too, and recorded in the org's security trail as role probing.
A bidder that drops out loses access in one action, by removing its grant or the role itself. The next request is refused. The audit of everything it read stays.
Ending a bidder's access at once
One customer in fifty, as a bidder reads them, with no name and with the email's name part and the phone's digits masked.
The seller acts as every role it holds again, to see what the bidders did.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomSignedI: Signed in, an analyst of bidder A sees what bidder_a is granted: the aggregate views, the profiles, the masked sample and the seller's records without a single customer identity. No customer's name, and no business or deal name from the CRM, is there to read.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultAnswer: The answer, in one point-in-time query. For each date on which anything about the customer was loaded, you see the version of each system's values in force at that time, and since when. From 1 September to 15 November, the two systems disagreed about where the customer lived.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultArrive: Every row either system received for Alfreds Futterkiste. The order system heard of its move on 1 September 1997; the CRM sent the old address again on 1 October, and the move on 15 November.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultCrm.de: The CRM holds the same customers as accounts, with each contact's email, which the order system never had. Its addresses can differ from the order system's, and for a while they do.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultGraphq: The business vault view is a GraphQL field too, filtered to the customer and ordered by time.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultHub.de: One row for each customer either system knows. Each row has the customer's code, the hash key of that code (which every link and satellite joins on), the system the customer was first seen in, and when.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultInsert: The customer table is insert-only, as a vault's staging receives it. A change arrives as a new row with its load date, and nothing is overwritten.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultLineag: The lineage of the mart's columns traces each one back through the point-in-time view and the satellites to the source field it came from.
Where a mart column comes from
Links pair the hubs' hash keys: a customer placed an order, an order contains a product. The relationships between them let GraphQL and Cypher walk the vault from hub to link to hub.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultMasked: The SQL explorer now runs as the European analyst. Personal data lives in the satellites, so that's where it's governed. As the analyst, the CRM satellite shows only European customers. Their contacts are withheld, and the names in their emails and the digits of their phone numbers are hidden. The hubs and links stay readable, so the analyst can still join on them.
Masked where the personal data is
de/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultProduc: The product satellite keeps Chai's old name beside Chai Tea, and Chang's price before and after its correction.
A renamed product, a corrected price
Two live systems and a data vault over them, declared as views: hubs, links and satellites with every version kept, refreshed by the engine as rows arrive, governed in the satellites, and queried point-in-time in SQL, GraphQL and REST, with lineage back to the source fields.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultRest.d: The current-state customer dimension, built on the vault, is a REST endpoint, so a downstream application reads it without knowing the vault is there.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultSatell: A satellite keeps each system's attributes for the customer. Every version is a row, with its load date and a hashdiff over its values. The CRM's resend on 1 October has the same hashdiff as the row before it, so it doesn't count as a new version.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultScenar: An order system and a CRM, both from Northwind, each keep their own copy of every customer. You want to know what was known about a customer, from which source, and when. A data vault answers that by keeping every version from every source. Here the vault is declared as views, and the engine builds and refreshes it. There's no ETL platform, job server or pipeline code to run. The work runs on the engine, where it scales, and one declared vault feeds the marts, the governed APIs and the lineage.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultWalk.d: The walk goes hub to link to hub, through the customer, its orders, the products in them, and every version of each product's name and price.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.filesAnswer.des: The stored view complaints_near_construction counts, for each neighborhood, the complaints made at an address with an active permit. Look at which neighborhood comes first.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.filesComplaints: complaints is one table over every file named complaints_*.csv in the folder. Each month's file is part of it; a new month's file needs no table of its own.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.filesDone.descr: A folder of files became a governed catalog: tables, relationships, an ontology term and a stored view, with nothing loaded. A new month's complaints file needs no new table, because the glob already names it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.filesDone.title: A folder became a catalog
de/tour.json::tour.steps.filesFormats.de: building_permits is read from a Parquet file, as the budget is from an Excel workbook and the inspections from a JSON file. Each is a governed table like any other.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.filesIntro.desc: A city publishes its open data as files: 311 complaints in a CSV file a month, building permits in Parquet, the budget in Excel and inspections in JSON. drop is one files source over that folder. Every file is a table, read where it lies, with no load step. The city wants to know which neighborhoods have the most complaints near active construction.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.filesJoin.descr: The relationship DRAWS joins a building permit to the complaints made at its address. The view that answers the question joins along it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.filesJoin.title: Complaints at permitted addresses
de/tour.json::tour.steps.filesMonths.des: The complaints counted by month. Each month comes from its own file, read as one table. Look for one row for each monthly file.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.filesRest.descr: The same view as a REST call. Every table and view is served over REST, GraphQL and SQL alike, under the same rules.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.filesRest.title: The same answer over REST
de/tour.json::tour.steps.filesTerm.descr: The ontology defines an open complaint as one the city has not yet closed. Terms like this say what the catalog's data means.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.filesTerm.title: What an open complaint is
de/tour.json::tour.steps.groupexposureAl: Each borrower's own exposure, as the bank's books see it. The largest is under 10% of Tier 1, so no borrower is anywhere near the 25% limit.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.groupexposureAn: The view group_exposure rolls every facility up to its borrower's group, through the owner's LEI and Wikidata. The Veolia and Vinci groups each pass 25% of Tier 1, and a joint venture owned by Veolia and EPH counts in both. Neither the bank's books nor Wikidata shows that alone. The borrowers and their loans are fictional.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.groupexposureEx: The same view in GraphQL: the groups the bank lends most to, their borrowers, what is committed, and whether each is over the limit.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.groupexposureFa: Every term loan, revolving credit facility and guarantee the bank has lent, with the borrower, what is committed and what is drawn. The limit counts what is committed.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.groupexposureGr: For each owner the bank records, the company at the top of its chain of parent organizations on Wikidata, found with one SPARQL property path. Wikidata knows a Czech holding company belongs to Veolia, or to E.ON, even though the bank's books do not.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.groupexposureJo: The bank's owners table and Wikidata's tables share the owner's LEI, and these relationships join them. The bank's data stays in its database and Wikidata's in its replica; the join happens in the query.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.groupexposureRe: A fictional bank's loan book and public linked data from Wikidata, joined by LEI in one governed model. Wikidata's ownership chains turn many small loans into a few large group exposures, and the answer is served in SQL, GraphQL and REST.
The view is a REST endpoint too, here grouped by whether a group is over the limit and summed on the server, ready for a risk report or a spreadsheet.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.groupexposureSc: A Prague bank lends to companies and records the company that owns each one by its Legal Entity Identifier (LEI). EU rules cap what it may lend to one client, or to a group of companies one owner controls, at 25% of its Tier 1 capital. It needs to know which groups it is over that limit to. Its books name each borrower's owner, not who owns the owner. The bank, its borrowers and its loans are fictional; the groups that own them are real.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.groupexposureTe: The glossary explains the terms a risk officer works with: large exposure, Tier 1 capital, Legal Entity Identifier and parent organization. A group of connected clients is companies that are one risk because one controls the others.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.groupexposureWi: Wikidata, the public knowledge graph, records each company's LEI and its parent organization. This source reads it through Wikidata's SPARQL query service. Its tables were landed once, when the demo was built, so the demo never calls Wikidata while you use it.
Who owns the owners, from Wikidata
de/tour.json::tour.steps.hasuramigration: BUYS_FOR joins a customer to their Salesforce account, approved like the relationships the import carried. From here the account is one field away from every customer, in every interface, under every role's rules.
One more relationship

Analysts can read order totals and account links, but no names or emails, and never cancelled orders. Those are the row rule and column lists the import carried over. The SQL explorer now runs as analyst. One SQL statement over the store and Salesforce gives revenue by the industry of the account behind each order. The analyst's rules apply as they do in GraphQL: cancelled orders are left out, and no name or email is read.
Revenue by industry

Admin › Import read the app's Hasura metadata export and showed what it became before applying anything. Carried as it is: the tables, their custom names, every relationship, the select, insert, update and delete permissions as row rules, column grants and write grants. Mapped to a better Provisa feature, each saying why: the inherited role, the action as a command, the event trigger as a trigger on the table's changes, the session variable and the claim that supplies it. Redo by hand, each saying what to do: the computed field and the trigger retries.
One import, and it works

Ana is a customer. Her token carried x-hasura-user-id: 1, and Provisa reads that claim as the session value hasura_user_id, which the imported row rules compare against. The role picker is now on ana. The storefront's order-history query, reshaped once for Provisa. The root field carries its domain, the column names follow Provisa's convention, and order_by is a list. The relationships items and product kept their Hasura names. Run as Ana, it answers her four orders and no one else's.
The order history, reshaped

Hasura's customers_by_pk becomes a filter on the table. The full_name computed field is the two names the screen puts together, and the import listed it as one to redo by hand. The row rule still limits Ana to her own row.
A read by key

The Hasura app imported in one step and worked at once, with its tables, names, relationships, roles, row rules, write permissions, the action and the triggers. The queries changed shape once and the rules not at all. One relationship later, the app reads its Salesforce accounts beside its orders, with nothing to keep in sync.
What you saw
The sales team keeps its accounts in Salesforce. Provisa registers the org as a source and its Account object as a table. Each business customer in the store names the account it buys for.
Joining Salesforce

An outfitter's storefront and support desk ran on Hasura v2 over this PostgreSQL database: customers, the catalog, orders and their lines, with roles for customers, support staff and analysts. The team moves the app to Provisa, and gains the sales team's Salesforce accounts beside the orders, under the same rules.
An app moving off Hasura

Support staff can read every order and every customer, as their Hasura permissions allowed. The role picker is now on support. The support desk's order screen, reshaped, now shows the Salesforce account beside each order's customer, with its industry and city, in the same request. Customers without an account show none.
Orders with their accounts

The four tables came over with the names the app uses. customers keeps Hasura's custom names givenName and familyName, the products table keeps its root name catalog, and each column carries the roles that may read it, from the select permissions.
The tables, as the app knew them
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderAsContro: Next, the SQL explorer runs as every role again.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderAsReview: Next, the SQL explorer runs as reviewer_ben, the first-level reviewer of the trading, research and operations desks.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderAudit.de: ops.queries records who ran every statement, as which role, over which table. The reviewer's reads of the queue and the watch list are here, as are yours.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderCustomer: SQL patterns check the same mail for customer data, meaning social security and account numbers. The customer table's columns are tagged pii, so this read is itself recorded.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderDone.des: Watch-list deals were matched against outbound mail by name and by meaning, ranked for review, and the list itself was never shown to the reviewer. This is post-review analytics behind real-time controls and does not replace data-loss prevention. Attachments, images, encoded text and personal channels are outside it. Monitoring employees needs disclosure and, in places, a works-council agreement.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderDone.tit: What this is, and is not
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderIntro.de: Northgate Partners, an invented bank, keeps a watch list of the deals it is working on. It wants to know whether anyone is sending deal-sensitive or customer data out of the bank. The answer reads three systems at once. bank is its Postgres database: the employees and their desks, the customers and who read their records. Every name and record here is generated.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderLeak.des: Two of the messages behind the queue. A trader not on deal Falcon tells a personal address about it in his own words, with no name, ticker or code name, and it ranks near the top. The deal team's mail to the deal's counsel names everything, and ranks low.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderLeak.tit: A paraphrase outranks the expected mail
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderMail.des: messages holds the employees' sent mail from Microsoft 365, each message in its sender's mailbox, with who sent it, when, and its text. Its recipients are in message_recipients; the bank's staff list and the personal mail providers in Postgres tell inside, outside and personal addresses apart.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderMailSour: mail is the bank's Microsoft 365 mail, every employee's mailbox, in the same message and recipient tables a Google Workspace source gives. This demo reaches no real tenant: the mailbox ships with the demo as the source's stored copy, which never refreshes.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderMatch.de: deal_match is what the match_deals command found. For each message and deal, it records whether it names the company, an alias, the ticker or the code name, and how close it reads to the deal's description through a local embedding model. A paraphrase that avoids every name still scores.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderOverTheW: Who was brought over the wall for the deal, and so who could have known of it. The flagged sender is not among them.
Was the sender over the wall?
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderPiiAcces: ops.pii_access lists every read of a pii-tagged table, here the read you just made. The queue does the same for the bank's staff from the bank's own access log. The operations employee who read customer records that week and then mailed customer data out ranks first.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderQueue.de: One materialized view ranks every case. The match is weighted by context: a sender outside the deal's team, a recipient outside the bank or at a personal address, and a message sent before the announcement raise it; a deal-team member writing to the deal's own counterparties lowers it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderReviewer: Read as the reviewer, the same queue holds only the cases of the desks they review, with the flagged entity shown and the deal withheld. Row rules on the mail and its matches do this; nothing is copied. The watch list itself is refused to them.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderWatchLis: deal is the watch list, the workbook's sheet of deals, with each deal's company, the names it goes by, its ticker, its project code name and whether it is public yet. It is the most restricted table here. The control room reads it, a deal team only its own deal, and a first-level reviewer never.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderWhyFlagg: Polly helps the human reviewer after the fact. Its answer was made when the demo was built, and is shown as stored.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderWorkbook: control_room is an Excel workbook the control room keeps itself. Each sheet is a table: the deals in discussion, who was brought over the wall for each, the deals' counterparties, and which deals each message is screened against. Provisa reads the file where it lies.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceAnswer: The view exposure_by_county joins the book to the risk in each county, and is kept stored. Ordered by insured value weighted by risk percentile, it puts the counties where the most exposure meets the highest risk first.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceBook.d: Each policy in force, with its county, line of business, total insured value, premium and deductible.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceByRati: Grouped by FEMA's risk rating, the same view shows how much of the book's insured value sits in counties rated Relatively High or Very High.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceGovdat: The government data comes from AskAmerica.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceJoin.d: The book and the public risk tables share the county's FIPS code, and these relationships join them. Every query that crosses them uses this join.
You saw the insurer's own data joined by county to public risk data, all in one governed model. One view answers where the exposure meets the risk, in SQL, GraphQL and REST, and each role sees only what it's allowed to.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceRest.d: The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped and summed on the server. Any client that speaks HTTP gets the answer without writing SQL.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceRisk.d: Every US county's all-hazard risk score and rating, its national percentile, its expected annual loss and the value of all its buildings. The wildfire and storm tables sit beside it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceScenar: A property insurer wants to know where its exposure is concentrated against natural-hazard risk. Its own book of policies, with the total insured value of each, is in its database; the hazard risk of every US county is public, in FEMA's, the US Forest Service's and NOAA's data. The tour shows Provisa joining the two, by county, and answering the question in SQL, over REST and in GraphQL.
The ontology names what an underwriter asks about: total insured value, accumulation, probable maximum loss and expected annual loss. Here, accumulation means exposure concentrated where one event can reach many policies.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsAllocati: Every allocation the fund made, with the county, the fiscal year, the program area, the provider paid, what was awarded and what has been spent. Staff see every row; the public role sees none.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsAnswer.d: The view treatment_against_burden joins the fund's treatment and recovery spending to each county's deaths, and is kept stored. Ordered by deaths for each million dollars spent, it puts the counties where the money meets the most deaths first.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsAsPublic: The SQL explorer now runs as the resident role, the role the council's dashboard and residents use. The statements that follow see only what it allows.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsByRegion: Grouped by the fund's five regions, the dashboard shows how many residents each has and how much treatment and recovery was spent there.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsDeaths.d: Overdose deaths per 100,000 residents in each county in 2023. Where a county had 1 to 9 deaths, CDC suppresses the count and publishes a modelled rate instead, flagged here, so every county has a rate to compare.
The government data comes from AskAmerica: CDC's overdose deaths and death rates, the Census Bureau's population and USAspending's federal spending, each by county.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsJoin.des: The fund's counties and the public tables share the county's FIPS code, and these relationships join them. Every query that crosses them uses this join.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsPublic.d: The council's dashboard is the view overdose_burden_by_county, run here as the resident role. It shows each county's residents, deaths, death rate and federal money per resident, and reads none of the fund's allocations or the providers paid.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsRecap.de: The fund's own records and public health and census data, joined by county in one governed model. Two stored views answer the question: the staff's, which reads the fund's spending, and the public's dashboard, which reads none of it. Each is served in SQL, GraphQL and REST to the roles allowed to read it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsRest.des: The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped and summed on the server, so a council website or a spreadsheet can read the dashboard over HTTP.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsScenario: A state opioid settlement fund pays Ohio's 88 counties for treatment, recovery, prevention and naloxone. The council asks which counties have the most overdose deaths for the treatment the money pays for. The fund's allocations are in its own database; deaths, population and federal spending are public. The fund and its figures are made up; the counties and the public data are real.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsTerms.de: The ontology explains the terms a council member or a resident will meet: settlement fund, abatement, allocation, expenditure, suppressed count and rate per 100,000. Here, abatement means what the settlements require the money to be spent on.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaAnswer.de: The view product_risk joins each product's stock to its shortage, its manufacturer's ongoing recalls and its Medicaid prescriptions, and is kept stored. The critical products at risk come first, fewest days of supply first.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaByRisk.de: Grouped by risk, the same view shows how many products face a shortage, a recall or both, the stock they hold and how often Medicaid prescribes them.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaFormulary: Each product the pharmacy stocks, with its NDC, generic name, manufacturer, therapeutic class and whether it is critical. Its stock at each site sits beside it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaGovdata.d: The government data comes from AskAmerica.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaJoin.desc: The formulary meets the shortages and Medicaid's prescriptions by NDC. A recall names its firm, not its NDC, so the vendor master records each manufacturer's FDA firm name, and this relationship joins it to the recalls.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaJoin.titl: Joined by NDC and by firm
de/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaRecap.des: You saw the pharmacy's own data joined by NDC and by firm to public drug data, all in one governed model. One view answers which products are at risk, in SQL, GraphQL and REST, and each role sees only what it's allowed to.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaRest.desc: The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped and summed on the server. Any client that speaks HTTP gets the answer without writing SQL.
A hospital pharmacy wants to know which of its products face shortage or recall risk. Its formulary and the stock each site holds are in its own database; FDA's drug shortages and recalls and Medicaid's prescriptions are public. The tour shows Provisa joining the two and answering the question in SQL, GraphQL and REST.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaShortages: Every shortage FDA has posted, one row per package, with its status, the product's availability and its NDC product code. The recalls and Medicaid's prescriptions sit beside it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaTerms.des: The ontology names what a pharmacy buyer asks about: NDC, formulary, drug shortage, recall class and days of supply. Here, supply risk means a shortage, a recall by the product's maker, or too few days of stock on hand.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingAnswer: The view customer_columns keeps each customers column as the latest run found it, emptiest first. A fifth of the customers never answered the marketing question; some emails are missing and some hold a name instead; signup dates start at a 1900-01-01 placeholder, and lifetime values run from refunds below zero to test accounts at 999,999.99.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingCountr: The five most common values in the country column. US, USA and United States are one country, written three different ways in just these five. A count by country would split it into three.
Setup ran the profiler twice, and between the runs the CRM's next sync wrote every US postal code as ZIP+4. The drift table compares each measure with the previous run's. The measures postal_code's change moved are flagged drifting, and the columns the sync left alone are not.
What changed since the last run
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingDuplic: The model declares customer_id the key, but the export held no constraint, and 150 customers are in it twice, every field the same. The profile counts the repeated rows and the key values held by more than one row.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingMember: The customers and orders tables are members of the profiler. From a member's editor you can run a profile at once or view its runs, each with its rows and how long it took.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingOrigin: Ten customers as the CRM holds them. Next, the same statement in an environment generated from the profile.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingPhones: Each phone number reduced to its shape, where a digit becomes 9. The CRM never checked the format, so one column holds four of them, which a join or a dialer would have to reconcile first.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingProfil: A profiler holds only a schedule and its run settings. This one runs every night at 02:00. Its first run was made when the demo was built, so the results are already here.
You saw the acquired company's tables and a profile of them made by the built-in profiler and kept as governed tables. Nulls, ranges, formats, plausible types and duplicates each answer what is in this data, in SQL, GraphQL and REST, and each role sees only what it's allowed to.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingRest.d: The view is a REST endpoint too. A data quality tool or a migration script gets the profile without writing SQL.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingRuns.d: A run's results land as tables of their own, one for each kind of measure, and every run is kept beside the ones before it. Here are the customers table's runs, with the rows each read and the repeated rows it found.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingScenar: An outdoor retailer has bought a smaller one, Harbor Outfitters, and received its CRM's customers and orders. Before anyone builds on them, it needs to know what is in this data. Provisa's built-in Data Profiler answers it, and its results are governed tables like any other, read in SQL, GraphQL and REST.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingStrata: The share of rows each postal_code value holds in each run, the oldest at the back. The newest run is flagged as drifting, as the drift table showed, and the run before it is not.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingSynthe: In synthetic, every row the same statement returns was generated from the customers' profile, with the same columns, value shapes and spread, and none of the real customers. The profile is enough to generate test data from.
The ontology defines data profile, plausible type, value shape, duplicate row and placeholder value, and ties each term to the measures it describes.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingTerrai: Opening the customers table's profile runs on the terrain
The latest run of customers drawn as terrain, with one ridge for each column, its height the rows in each range of values, and each column's nulls in front of it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingToProd: Next, the switcher returns to prod.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingToSynt: Next, the switcher moves to synthetic, a Test (synthetic) environment.
The profile infers what a column holds from its values, its name and its tags: an email, a phone number, a postal code, an identifier. Each comes with its confidence and the evidence for it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningAsD: Now as the data science role, whose feature store needs the orders but not the margins.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningAsF: The SQL explorer now runs as the finance role, the team that reads margins in full.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningClo: close_by_category, finance's close, may be read only from 02:00 to 02:15 UTC. Outside it this read is refused, naming the view and when its window next opens. Inside the window it returns the close instead.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningDat: On the same dataset and the same query, cost and margin read 0, and service orders are gone (a row rule).

order_margins has every order with its revenue, cost and margin. It keeps every version of every row, so a team can read it as of any moment, and that's what a team pulls. Its load window says when users and clients may read it. Here that's all day except 00:00 to 00:30 UTC. A real warehouse would usually open a narrower overnight window; the demo's is wide so you can walk through it at any hour.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningFee: Orders arrive on Kafka a few a second, after a month of history; prices and stock counts on their own topics. Each lands into the warehouse's own table within seconds, and each landing refreshes the datasets built on it.
The feeds, landed as they arrive
de/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningFin: The latest orders as finance reads them, with revenue, cost and margin in every category.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningJoi: An order names its product, and the product knows its cost and category. The dataset joins each order to its product. The close is a view over that view, built on the dataset plus the stock and price feeds and refreshed in turn.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningNot: Inside the window a scheduled trigger writes a notice for each team: finance every five minutes, data science two minutes later. The notices table's live Kafka output publishes each to the topic dataset-ready. The notice's time is the dataset's version time.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningPul: Each team's consumer reads the notice and pulls the whole dataset over Arrow Flight as recorded at its version time, meaning the orders that had landed by then, so neither a refresh landing mid-pull nor an order landed later can change what it reads. It records the rows, the seconds and the rows a second.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningRec: Feeds landed as they arrived, and datasets were built and refreshed from them. Each team was told on Kafka when a dataset was ready, and pulled it over Arrow Flight as of that moment, seeing only what its role allows and only inside the dataset's window, with no copies and no extraction jobs.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningRes: How many pulls each team made and how fast they ran on average, grouped on the server.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningSce: A coffee roaster's warehouse takes three feeds (orders, prices and stock counts) and builds datasets from them as they land. Two teams downstream need the big one, every order with its margin: finance for its reporting, data science for its feature store. They want it as soon as it is ready, with no copies and no extraction jobs.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningWar: Its products and what each costs, the notices it sends when a dataset is ready, and the pulls the teams' consumers record.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityAdmitted: Every silver row carries the run id of the checks that admitted its batch. The relationship ADMITTED_BY joins it to those checks in dq_results.
From a row to the checks that admitted it
de/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityBronze.d: bronze holds every batch as it landed, never changed. Clean data is typed on landing: the sale id, when it was sold, the quantity. The messy fields, shop code, product and price, stay raw until silver.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityBronze.t: Bronze: typed where it is clean
de/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityChecks.d: dq_results is a materialized view that computes the checks in SQL on every landed batch, counting the rows that fail each and marking it pass or fail. Batch 1 passes them all; batch 2 fails three.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityDone.des: Landing a batch refreshed the checks, silver and gold, and nothing else had to run. The clean batch reached gold. The bad one stopped at bronze, and you can find out why with a query.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityGold.des: Gold is one GROUP BY over silver that gives sales, items, revenue and the price range by day and product, from checked data only.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityIntro.de: A chain of five shops sends its sales as a daily feed. Each batch lands as the bronze layer in sales, the chain's database. Everything after bronze is a materialized view (the checks, silver and gold), and landing a batch is enough to refresh them all. You need to know whether to trust this data before it reaches gold.
Gold, silver and the checks are one data product: the totals consumers read, the sales behind them, and the evidence each batch passed. Bronze stays out.
A data product to hand on
de/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityRaw.desc: The first batch's products as they landed, with one product in several spellings, such as COFFEE, Coffee and cofee. Silver makes them one.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityRaw.titl: Raw, as the feed spelled it
The rows of batch 2 that fail a check, still in bronze as they landed: a shop the chain does not have, negative quantities, prices that are not numbers. None of batch 2 reaches silver; batch 1 stays.
What the bad batch failed on
de/tour.json::tour.steps.qualitySilver.d: Silver is bronze cleaned up, built only from the batches that passed. Shop codes are trimmed and upper-cased, each product has one spelling, the price is a number, the day is worked out, and a sale sent twice is kept once, in its latest version.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityWhichChe: A silver sale and, along ADMITTED_BY, every check of the run that admitted it. Each one passed, with no failing rows.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceAsFile: This is the time the report was first built and filed, taken from the answer in the refreshes step. It falls after the filed figures were entered and before the correction was. The report is now read as Provisa had it recorded at that time, so nothing recorded later can change it.
As recorded when it was filed
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceAsOf.d: The report as of its business date shows what the figures were for 30 September.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceAsOfNo: Read as Provisa has it recorded today, 30 September shows the corrected figure, 1,550,000 for the rates desk. That is the figure in the books now, and it differs from what was filed.
As of 30 September, as recorded now
The audit log records who ran every read, as which role, and the time it read the report as of and as recorded at. The regulator's reproduction is itself on record.
Who read it, and as of when
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceBook.d: Each position, with its desk, its notional in its own currency and the rate it converts to USD at, valid from 30 September. One of these rates is corrected after the report is first filed.
As of 30 September and as recorded when it was filed, the rates desk reads 1,540,000, the figure the regulator received. The correction recorded since does not change what was filed.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceImpact: Rename fx_rate here, and Provisa lists what reads it before you save, the report among them.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceLineag: The report's exposure column, traced back. Each desk's exposure is the sum of notional times fx_rate over its positions. Every column of the report leads to the source columns it is computed from.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceNow.de: Each desk's exposure as the report stands today, with when Provisa recorded each figure. The rates desk reads 1,550,000: the corrected rate.
One report, explained and reproduced: its figure traced to its source columns and the refresh that built it, the impact of a change named before it is made, the report as filed beside the report now, and every read of it in the audit log.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceRefres: Each build of the report records what it was built from: the version of the report's definition, and the version of its input with how that was established. There are two builds, one as first filed and one after the correction.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceScenar: A bank files an exposure report with its regulator for 30 September. The regulator asks where the rates desk's figure came from, and for the report exactly as it was filed, because a rate has been corrected since. The bank's trading book is read live from its own database.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAccess.de: Everything the group holds about the person behind each access request, from both subsidiaries, in one query. Amélie Fournier is a member in the EU and in the US.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAsAdmin.d: Next, the SQL explorer runs as every role again.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAsAnalyst: The second layer is security: the data steward's rules decide what each reader gets, by role and by the reader's region. They are applied in the home region, before anything leaves it. Next, the role picker switches to group_analyst, who works on group reporting in the US, so the SQL and GraphQL after this run as group_analyst.
The data steward's rules, as a group analyst
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAsDpo.des: Next, the SQL explorer runs as dpo, who answers data subject requests.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAsEuRevie: Next, the SQL explorer runs as reviewer with region__eu, a reviewer whose region is the EU.
As a reviewer in the EU
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAsReviewe: Next, the SQL explorer runs as reviewer, the group's insider review.
The SQL explorer now runs as marketing_eu. The steward's rule lets EU marketing read the EU customers who agreed to marketing, and only them. The view is built in the EU from EU rows.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAudit.des: Every statement the tour ran, in one audit trail across both regions: who ran it, on what, and which region answered it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailEngines.d: Federation has a tab for each region, and each region runs its own engine. So one config gives two data processing environments. You are on the US node. It reads EU data only through the EU's store, never from a copy of its own.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailErasure.d: For each erasure request, every row the group deletes, with its subsidiary, its table and its key. Each subsidiary deletes its own rows, in its own region.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailEuCustome: The EU customers. The table's region is the EU, so its replicas and cache live only in the EU's store. Homing decides where the rows live. It does not decide who may read them. That is the next layer.
An EU table, homed in the EU
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailEveryRole: Next, the role picker switches back to All.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailGroupGrap: The same group view over GraphQL, under the same rules.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailGroupView: Every loyalty customer of the group. US customers appear as they are. EU customers appear by a pseudonym, because the steward's rule says a reader outside the EU gets no name or address. The EU applied that rule before its rows left, and the record of this query names the EU as the region that answered.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailJoin.desc: A request joins to each subsidiary's customers by email address. That is how one request finds the same person in both.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailJoin.titl: How a request finds a person
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailLimits.de: These features can support meeting the GDPR's rules on where data lives and who reads it, but they do not make a group compliant. That takes active design by people who know the data protection and cross-border transfer rules that apply. The lawful basis, the impact assessment, retention and any works-council agreement remain the group's own legal process.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailLimits.ti: What this is, and is not
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailOrgRegion: The organization holds both regions. Each row names the stores used there: the region's engine, and where its replicas, views, cache, build state and record are kept. EU data is processed with the EU's own stores.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailPlatformR: The platform's config declares the regions, here the EU and the US, and grants them to the organization. Each region has its own data processing: its own engine and its own stores. The EU's purpose is residency, for customer data that must stay in the European Union. In this sandbox you can read this page but not change it.
The legend explains each purpose. A purpose says why a region exists. It does not move data or decide who reads it. Two layers do that, and the tour shows each: homing, the engine's rules about where data lives, and security, the data steward's rules about who reads what.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailQueue.des: EU staff's outbound mail, scored in the EU: a personal address, customer records attached, a bulk export. The queue carries the score, the signals and a pseudonym of the sender. No message text leaves the EU, and the sender is withheld.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailRecap.des: One config granted two regions, each with its own engine and stores: two data processing environments. Homing kept the EU tables, their replicas and their cache in the EU. The data steward's rules decided what each reader got, by role and by the reader's region, and the EU applied them before anything left it. Group reporting read EU customers pseudonymised, EU marketing read only consenting customers, access and erasure were each one query, the sender was revealed only to a reviewer in the EU, and every read is in one record.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailRegions.d: The US subsidiary's database is homed in the US, and the EU subsidiary's in the EU. Homing is the engine's rule about where data lives. A homed table's replicas and cache stay in its home region, and other regions reach it only through that region.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailRegions.t: Homing: each source names its home
The group's register records who asked to see their data, who asked to have it erased, and when. It holds no customer data itself.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailReveal.de: The same queue. The steward's mask on the sender column reveals the sender only to a reviewer whose assigned region is the EU (region__eu). Everyone else reads it withheld. What a reader gets depends on their region as well as their role, and no role was made for the combination.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.retailReveal.ti: The sender, revealed in the EU
A retail group runs an EU and a US subsidiary as one business. The tour asks whether it can do that without breaking GDPR. Each subsidiary keeps its own database. This is the EU one, with its loyalty customers, their marketing consent, orders, staff and the mail staff send outside the group.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsBatteryD: The shop's first question, in SQL: the reviews that say "battery dies", counted by product, with each product's ratings. One statement reads an Elasticsearch search and two MongoDB tables, and a handful of products stand out.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsBoughtWi: The second question asks in Cypher for the products rated under three stars and what their buyers also bought. The graph runs across the MongoDB ratings and the Neo4j purchases, and power banks keep turning up.

The same result, grouped by degree to answer the question it was drawn for. The groups bring out the products most often bought together with the low-rated ones, and a bigger number means more pairings run through that product. Degree is counted within this result only: the products rated under three stars, and what five or more of their customers also bought. The red nodes are the products. The ratings and the pair nodes are grouped too.
An electronics shop wants to know which products disappoint, and what their buyers do about it. The answer is spread over three NoSQL stores. This one, catalog, is MongoDB: a document for each product, its specs nested, and the star ratings customers give.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsCypherTa: bought_together is a Cypher query against Neo4j, registered as a table. For each product it lists every other product its buyers bought, and how many of them did.
A Cypher query as a table
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsDone.des: Three NoSQL stores, a MongoDB pipeline, an Elasticsearch search and a Cypher query, joined on the product and asked the shop's question in SQL, Cypher, REST and GraphQL.
This example query reads the battery complaints in GraphQL, with each review's highlighted text and its product nested beneath it through the relationship.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsGraphSto: purchases is Neo4j, holding 2,000 customers, each linked by a BOUGHT relationship to the products they bought. All three stores name a product by the same id.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsJoin.des: Relationships join the tables on the product id across all three stores. COMPLAINS_ABOUT joins a matching review to its product in the catalog, so a query reaches from Elasticsearch to MongoDB without spelling out the join.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsPipeline: ratings_by_product is a MongoDB aggregation pipeline, registered as a table. It groups the star ratings by product and gives each product's count, average and one-star ratings. A query reads it like any other table.
A MongoDB pipeline as a table
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsRest.des: The same search as a REST call, its phrase passed as a parameter. Every surface Provisa serves reads the same governed tables, so REST answers as SQL and GraphQL do, under the same rights.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsSearchSt: reviews is Elasticsearch, holding the 5,000 reviews customers wrote, each with its product, its stars and its text.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsSearchTa: reviews_matching is an Elasticsearch search, registered as a table. A query sets its phrase parameter, and each row is a review whose text holds the phrase, with the phrase highlighted.
An Elasticsearch search as a table
de/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsDone.des: Shakespeare's lines went from Postgres rows to Qdrant vectors, governed searches and a graph of echoes and themes.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsEchoNetw: Cypher draws the lines that closely echo a line of another sonnet, and the sonnets they are in. Look for the sonnets joined by more than one echo.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsEchoes.d: The echo table. The command link_echoes asks the vector store for each line's three nearest lines in other sonnets and writes them here, each with its similarity.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsGraph.de: Three relationships make the tables a graph. A line is IN its sonnet, EVOKES a theme and ECHOES a line of another sonnet, with its score. Cypher walks them like any graph.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsIntro.de: Shakespeare's 154 sonnets are stored in Postgres, embedded into Qdrant, searched by meaning and grown into a graph. The tour asks which themes run through the sonnets and where Shakespeare echoes himself. sonnets is the Postgres source. It has a row for each sonnet and for each of the 2,155 lines.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsLines.de: The line table has a row for each of the 2,155 lines. The command embed_lines is a single governed SQL statement. Its embed() call turns each line's words into a vector, and the rows are written to Qdrant through the collection's write route.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsSearch.d: lines_like is a search table. Provisa runs the search live in Qdrant, using the arguments your statement passes, here a phrase and how many lines to return. Each line comes back with a score that says how close it is to the phrase.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsThemeVie: Each theme view stores one fixed search, joined back to the lines it found, with each line's score. This one holds the twenty lines nearest to "the ravages of time"; four more hold beauty, mortality, jealousy and verse that outlives death.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsThemesBy: For each theme, how many of the lines it found are in the Fair Youth sonnets and how many in the Dark Lady sonnets. Look for a theme that belongs to one sequence.
vectors is Qdrant. It holds one point for each line, and each point's vector is the embedding of that line's words. Provisa reads and writes it just as it does any other source.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step0.descripti:
🧭 This compass reopens the tour anytime. To leave, click the app or press Esc.

Provisa is one model that holds your data, its metadata and the processing between them. The same model defines your data estate and operates it, and it stays out of the data path.

So everything stays in sync and reuse is built in: a relationship, metric, mask or rule defined once serves every surface, environment and role. Duplicate tables and metrics, duplicate commands and rules, even two systems serving the same data sit side by side in the model, so duplication is easy to see and simple to remove.

It is compact, extensible and composable, and it sits beside what you already have.

🎯 The core is one short exercise: connect a database, then query it in the language or tool you already use, or ask in plain English. About five minutes, right from your desktop, with no infrastructure to stand up.

Natural LanguageSQLGraphQLCyphergRPCJSON:APIRESTMCPPostgres · pgwireNeo4j · BoltJDBC · Java/JVMArrow Flight SQL · ADBCDuckDB · airport

Everything after that is a Deep Dive you pick from a menu when you are ready.

Next, connect a source. →
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step0.title: Welcome, let's take the tour
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step1.descripti:
Everything you want to federate is registered here:
🗄️ Databases🏢 Warehouses🔌 APIs📄 Files☁️ SaaS

Provisa unifies them all into one queryable graph.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step1.title: Start with Sources
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step10.descript:
🧩 A spec-compliant JSON:API surface:

GET /data/jsonapi/pet-store/inquiries?page[size]=20

📄 Paging and 🔍 filtering out of the box.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step10.title: JSON:API (5 of 9 surfaces)
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step11.descript:
🌐 And a plain REST endpoint, described by OpenAPI:

GET /data/rest/pet-store/inquiries

📄 Fully described, so any REST client or code generator can consume it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step11.title: OpenAPI / REST (6 of 9 surfaces)
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step12.descript:
🤖 The seventh surface lets an agent reason with your data. It drives the same governed tools (search the catalog, describe tables, run SQL, follow relationships) and chains them to answer questions no single query could, every call bound by your role's governance.

🔌 The same MCP server plugs into Claude Desktop, Claude Code or any MCP client, so agents explore and reason over your model the governed way.

🔑 Uses your own LLM key; this exchange is a canned example.

Two more read the same governed data from Python. →
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step12.title: MCP (7 of 9 surfaces)
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step13.descript:
💬 "how many pets per species"

Ask in plain English and Provisa compiles your question into all seven at once. Each panel below is that one sentence as SQL, GraphQL, Cypher, gRPC, JSON:API and REST.

It can't open Python or the Notebook directly, but you can always ask Polly to move a query into either one.

🔑 Live natural-language queries use your own LLM key; this one's a canned example.

✅ One model behind all nine surfaces, and plain English writes the queries for you.

Natural LanguageSQLGraphQLCyphergRPCJSON:APIRESTMCPPythonNotebook
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step13.title: The surface that writes your queries
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step14.descript:
✅ You saw it end to end, one source queried in the language or tool you already use, or asked in plain English. You could stop here.

Everything else is a Deep Dive: connecting data, relationships, modeling, governance, querying, test data, publishing and operating. Done opens the Deep Dives catalog.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step14.title: That's the five-minute core
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step15.descript:
A relationship does two jobs. It shapes your data model: how tables across sources and domains connect, which every query surface follows, whether GraphQL nesting, Cypher paths or SQL joins.

It is also a rule. Joins are governed. A role without the ignore_relationships right can join only along registered relationships, so which ones exist decides which queries are legal. Grant that right deliberately to a role you trust and it joins freely (never in high-security mode).

Relationships link tables across sources, even across different databases, turning flat tables into a traversable graph.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step15.title: Connect the graph
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step16.descript:
🔗 Map a source column to a target column and set cardinality:
1 → 11 → ∞∞ → ∞

✨ Or let Provisa infer relationships for you with AI.

🛡️ Because a relationship is a rule, adding, changing or removing one can make a query legal or illegal. A relationship requested from outside the source table's domain, or by someone who may not create relationships, waits for approval.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step16.title: Define a relationship
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step17.descript: The entity-relationship diagram renders every registered table in your federated model and the relationships between them.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step17.title: See the ERD
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step18.descript:
🔐 Registering a table sets per-column access, wired straight into roles:
👁️ Read✏️ Write

That's role-based access control, and the roles themselves are defined here on the Security page.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step18.title: Access control (RBAC)
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step19.descript:
🔎 Once roles exist, go finer: restrict which rows each role sees with attribute-based predicates:

region = user.region AND status != 'archived'

📐 Data-driven and enforced per row, across every source and protocol.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step19.title: Row-level security
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step2.descripti: ➕ New connections start with this button: PostgreSQL, Snowflake, MongoDB, a REST API, a CSV, and the rest of the 82 connectors.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step2.title: Register a source
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step20.descript:
🔧 Compose your whole delivery pipeline right here, with no separate ETL tool:
  • 👁️ Views: over any table, ephemeral or materialized, and views over views.
  • ⚡ Commands: governed, typed operations (an HTTP service, a Python model, a stored procedure) that serve as a step inside your pipeline and as an API that downstream apps and agents call to act on your data, from every surface, governed and traced.
  • ⭐ Entities & facts: declare a dimension or fact once and Provisa generates the warehouse, methodology-neutral: 3NF (Inmon), star schema (Kimball), or Data Vault.
  • 📏 Metrics: governed aggregate definitions (“net revenue”) with grain bound at query time. Define once, and every surface (SQL, GraphQL, AI agents) computes the same number, and views built on a metric regenerate when its definition changes.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step20.title: Build your delivery pipeline
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step21.descript:
🏗️ Materialize a view and you get a full declarative ETL engine:
  • 📅 Scheduled snapshots on real business calendars: recurrence rules, holidays, business-day gating, and a close grace period, so it fires on your reporting calendar.
  • 🗄️ Store As…: replace, upsert, or keep history with snapshot / delta, plus incremental compute.
  • 🕰️ Time travel: bitemporal history; query the model as of any point in time.
  • ⚡ Near-real-time refresh with debounce, or freshness-driven republish as inputs change.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step21.title: Materialize into a live warehouse
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step22.descript:
🧬 Lineage is the dependency trail your derivations leave: what each view, calculated column or metric is built from, and what depends on it. This is a real query, analyzed. Follow name_upper back through its transforms to the exact source columns that feed it.

Nothing runs; the query is only analyzed.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step22.title: Lineage, end to end
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step23.descript:
The Admin pages run the platform:
  • ⚙️ Choose and configure your federation engine: DuckDB (embedded, zero-config), Trino, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, or a cloud warehouse as a first-class engine (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Synapse). Swap it anytime; the model, the surfaces and the governance above it never change.
  • 🔗 Whichever engine you pick brings its own live external data reach: Parquet, Iceberg and Delta read in place, zero-copy, credentials provisioned for you. Anything it can't link live lands as a governed replica.
  • 🔑 Manage encryption keys and wire up auth providers
  • 📊 Observability: send traces to any OpenTelemetry collector
  • 📤 Export the model's configuration, the whole model or chosen sections, as a file to review, diff and ship through CI/CD

The same model travels from local dev to production, validated at every step, with no rewrite:

  • Develop: embedded DuckDB, no Docker. Build & validate locally.
  • Validate at scale: Docker, spin up an engine + observability. Prove behavior against production engines.
  • Promote: point at your own infrastructure, build through CI/CD, ship to production.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step23.title: Operate it
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step3.descripti:
One picker lists every type, grouped by category: Subscriptions, RDBMS, Cloud DW, Analytics, Data Lake, NoSQL, Code Resolvers, Graph, File, API, Streaming, Enterprise, Data Quality, Other. Search by name or alias, or narrow with the category chips. Each type shows its logo and a reach icon: ⚡ read live in place, or a copy icon where Provisa reads a refreshed replica.

Pick one, fill the connection, Save.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step3.title: 83 source types, 14 categories
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step4.descripti:
Whatever the source, whether a Mongo collection, a Kafka topic, a REST endpoint or a graph, Provisa decomposes it into a 2D table: one uniform shape to query across every source.

📁 Group tables into domains, each owned by a data steward who guards the model's quality as it evolves.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step4.title: Everything becomes a table
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step5.descripti:
Choose a source, schema and table, then pick columns, each with its own policy:
  • 🎭 Masking: redact values per role
  • 👁️ Visibility: show or hide the column
  • 🏷️ Aliases: rename for the model

A source and a few tables is the whole setup. 🚀 Next, query it. →
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step5.title: Pick columns & policy
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step6.descripti:
SQL lives in the SQL explorer. Standard SQL federates across every source, so one statement can join Postgres to Mongo to a CSV. The model's own metadata and every activity trace are queryable tables here too, so you can join your audit log or lineage straight to live data.

🔌 The same governed model is served over several protocols besides this explorer; your tool picks the one it already speaks:

  • pgwire: every Postgres-compatible client (psql, DBeaver, Tableau, Power BI) connects out of the box.
  • JDBC: drops into any Java/JVM app, ETL pipeline or JDBC-capable BI tool.
  • Arrow Flight SQL: columnar streaming for ADBC clients, with no row re-encoding, built for large result sets.
  • DuckDB · airport: ATTACH Provisa from DuckDB and query the governed federation in place.
  • OData: Excel and Power BI connect through their built-in OData feed and read governed tables directly.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step6.title: SQL (1 of 9 surfaces)
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step7.descripti:
◈ The same query, typed as GraphQL:

{ inquiries { groupBy { user }, count } }

It groups and aggregates over your relationships, with 🎯 one endpoint and 📖 a self-documenting schema.

🔌 Call it from any GraphQL client, such as Apollo, Relay or urql. With federation enabled, Provisa joins an Apollo supergraph as a subgraph, so your federated model composes alongside your existing graphs.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step7.title: GraphQL (2 of 9 surfaces)
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step8.descripti:
🕸️ Traverse the federated model as a graph with Cypher:

MATCH (u:Users)-[:SUBMITTED]->(i:Inquiries)

↔️ That traversal runs across sources, with no single graph database required.

🔌 Any Bolt client, such as Neo4j Browser or Bloom, runs the same traversal over the wire, with no code change.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step8.title: Cypher (3 of 9 surfaces)
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step9.descripti:
⚙️ Every registered entity is also a gRPC service:

rpc QueryInquiries(...) returns (...)

Any gRPC client can call it, 📐 strongly typed and 🚀 high-throughput.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.step9.title: gRPC (4 of 9 surfaces)
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepBuildSource: The picker opened with its whole list, Parquet File was chosen and the form was filled in with the file's address (supplies.parquet). That is all a file source needs. This is only a look at the form: Next presses Cancel, and nothing is saved.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepCache.descr: 🗄️ These layers are separate. The response cache holds query results, and a request opts in with @cached or a SQL comment. Small lookup tables are mirrored to speed joins. A replica of a source table that cannot be attached lives in the durable store, beside materialized views.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepCache.title: Caches and replicas
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepCommands.de: ⚡ A command is a governed, typed operation, such as an HTTP service, a Python model or a stored procedure. Register it once and call it from every surface, with the same rights and tracing as a query.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepDataProduct:
📦 Every product here speaks ODPS (the Open Data Product Standard): owner, team, purpose, limitations, usage, SLA, support and custom properties. Provisa publishes it straight into Snowflake Horizon and BigQuery Dataplex, so it shows up as a native product in the catalog your consumers already use.

🔁 There is no separate export step. The spec is derived from the live model (tables, lineage, tags, ontology terms) every time, so what's published can't drift out of date.

✅ Publishing also sends an ontology extract, the part of your ontology that bears on what is published: the terms that define its columns, the broader and related terms they connect to, and the typed relationships between them. The data-quality results of the checkers that scan it go with it. A product's Related Terms panel lists its terms.
Data products, published where consumers already look
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepDomains.des: 🗂️ A domain groups tables, and its data steward governs that part of the model: who sees what, masks and row rules, sensitive data, and its ontology and data products.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepEnvKinds.de: An environment is a branch of your model, and the list shows which environment each one was made from. When you create one, you choose its data. Inherit copies each source's connection from the parent, so the tables show the parent's data. Unbound, the default, gives you the whole model with no connections, and you point each source at your own database. Test (fake) reads the parent's rows through each column's fake, and Test (synthetic) reads rows generated from the parent's profile runs. A connection value that references a secret or an environment variable is copied as that reference, so rotating the credential reaches every environment that uses it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepFakes.descr: 🎭 The Testing tab of a table's Columns shows each column's fake, such as email(). Fake only the identifying columns and keep the rest real. A column can also carry a synthetic rule, used only when generating synthetic data.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepFakes.title: Declare a fake
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepFakesFill.d: ✨ Fill from profile proposes fakes for identifying columns, and synthetic rules for the rest, from the table's latest profile. Nothing saves until you save the form.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepGlossary.de: 📖 Every term links to the columns that carry it and to other terms. Curate names, definitions, and typed relationships (kind-of, part-of, synonym-of) by hand, or let AI fill in the gaps from the ✨ menu: Definitions drafts only the terms still missing one, and Relationships proposes links across the whole ontology. Flag a term excluded from export to keep it out of published metadata.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepGlossaryTer: 📖 A term names one business concept, lists the columns that carry it, links to the terms it relates to and says what it means. Terms for real columns are derived for you; add one by hand for a concept no single column carries.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepMetrics.des: 📏 A metric is the business definition of a measure, an aggregate over one fact table. Define it once and SQL, GraphQL, the explore canvas and every view built from it compute the same number; a view regenerates when its metric changes.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepNotebook.de:
📓 The Notebook tab is JupyterLite, a Jupyter notebook running in your browser. Its first cell signs in, and the next reads the same statement as a DataFrame to chart or join with other data.

⬇️ Download the notebook and it opens in any desktop Jupyter, where the same cells read from Provisa as they do here.

The last surface writes your queries for you. →
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepObservabili: 🔭 Every request is traced, one span each. The trace feed lists your latest traces: filter them, pause the list, or open one to see its spans. Where your role may change settings, the Debug tracing tab adds a span per pipeline stage and per source call, for a set time.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPolly.descr:
💬 Polly sets Provisa up in plain language.

“register my Postgres” · “fake the email column in the customers table” · “create a QA environment on synthetic data” · “who can see salaries?”

Polly works through the same governed APIs and rights as the UI, so it can only do what you can. Polly is open here; the chat button reopens this panel anytime.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPolly.title: Meet Polly, your setup assistant
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPreview.des: 👀 Expand a row and click Preview for live data through the governed pipeline: masked, access-controlled, and server-paged, so even a billion-row table opens instantly. Filters, sorts, and grouping run inside the query, and API-backed tables prompt for their required parameters first.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepProductForm: 📦 Name the owner and team, the purpose, usage, SLA and support, then pick the tables and commands it contains. These are the fields that get published. A table joins a product only when both share the same domain.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepProfilerChe: Every run adds rows to its result tables: per-column measures (null share, distinct count, range), per-run measures (row count), children per parent, quantiles and drift. Once you register a result table, a data-quality checker can scan it like any other table. That checker is a Soda or Great Expectations source, so any measure a profile produces can carry a check that raises an issue. Drift is one such measure. Each run is compared with the table's recent runs, and a measure that moves is flagged. From the profiler's runs you can add an accepted constraint, a drift check, or a check against expectations from outside Provisa to the checker's contract.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPublish.des:
📤 Publish it where your org already looks. Catalog entries (tables, columns, domains, stewards, approved relationships), data products and column-level lineage go out, and each target receives what it supports: DataHub, OpenMetadata, Collibra, {{atlan}} and Apache Atlas as catalogs, Snowflake Horizon and BigQuery Dataplex as data-product listings, and lineage over OpenLineage.

Each entry on the Syncing page says its direction: Export sends to the tool, Import brings the tool's changes into Provisa, or both.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPublish.tit: Publish to the tools your org uses
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPython.desc:
🐍 The Python tab runs Python in your browser, signed in as you:

provisa_client.query('SELECT species, COUNT(*) …')

The answer comes back as a pandas DataFrame, read through the same governed pipeline, so your role's row rules and masks apply to it too.

🔌 The same provisa-client package installs with pip on any desktop Python, so a script written here runs unchanged in your own environment.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityPane: ✅ Write the contract by hand or build checks column by column (null rates, row counts, ranges, freshness) and dry-run it before saving. Every scan appends, so this table is the quality history, and you can chart it, alert on it or join it to anything.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityProd: ✅ A product's Data Quality panel lists the checker tables whose contracts scan its output ports, so a consumer sees the evidence next to the product. It is empty until a checker scans one. Data products are published in the Publish it Deep Dive.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityProf: 📊 A Data Profiler is a source that profiles its member tables on a schedule. Add a table to one on the Quality tab of the table's editor. Each run measures every column's shape, distributions and most common values, and how many children each parent has. Run Profile Now starts a run, and View Profile Runs shows the results. The results land as tables that you register and govern like any other, and nobody sees a profile until you register them. The next card puts checks on them.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityTabl: 🧪 A data-quality checker, Soda or Great Expectations, registers as a source. It scans back through Provisa's own postgres endpoint, so one contract dialect covers a Snowflake table, an Iceberg table and a Mongo collection alike. Its results land as an ordinary table, so expand the row and open it like any other.
A quality checker is just a source
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQuery.descr: 💬 You ask in the language or tool you already use (SQL, GraphQL, Cypher, plain language through Polly, or a BI tool or driver), and every one reads the same governed model, so the answer and the rules are the same whichever you pick.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQuery.title: Query it your way
🤖 The model and its relationships are available to AI agents (Polly, and agents connecting over MCP), and they shape the queries those agents write.

An agent runs under a role, so the same rule applies to it as to a person. A query that joins outside the registered relationships fails.

To let an agent discover relationships, grant its role the ignore_relationships right; to keep it inside guardrails, leave the role without it. It is the same deliberate grant as for a trusted identity (never honored in high-security mode).
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRelsList.de: 📋 Every relationship in the model, whether or not a source declares it. Filter and sort the list, and expand a row to edit a relationship or add its reverse. A role can join tables only along these relationships, unless it holds the ignore_relationships right.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRelsSuggest: ✨ The sparkle button looks for likely joins. It reads the foreign keys your sources declare and, when an AI model key is configured, asks the model to infer more. Nothing is declared until you accept a candidate, and a rejected one stays out until you clear the rejections.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepReports.des: 📊 The audit log you queried earlier also feeds ready-made reports (usage ranking, PII access, policy denials, query health), each a governed view in the ops domain. Adding your own takes one SQL statement, and it becomes a cataloged, exportable data product like any other table.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRequests.de: ✋ Someone who can't create relationships is asking to relate their tables to yours. They are often from another domain, and this is usually their first step toward asking for your data. Because relationships are governed, approving one changes which queries are legal. A role that may only join along approved relationships can now join across this one. A relationship request needs two approvals before it can run, and one that spans two domains needs a yes from each side. Approve it, run it, or reject it with a reason from a fixed list. Resolved requests move to the Resolved tab.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRoleInherit: 👪 A role can inherit from a parent. It receives the parent's grants, column visibility and row rules, and its own row rule for a table replaces the parent's. The role also carries its capabilities and its rate and complexity limits.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepScheduled.d: ⏱️ Run a webhook, a SQL statement or a command on a cron schedule, when a table changes, or on a table's error or quarantine. A trigger runs as a role you choose, so governance applies, and each shows how its last run ended.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepSynthetic.d: 🧪 In the Synthetic data tab, define a dataset from the profile runs of the tables you name and press Generate. It fills a non-production environment with rows shaped like those tables, with the same relationships and fan-out, at the scale you choose. A comparison report shows how close it came.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepSyntheticPr: 🔒 Declare a dataset private with a privacy budget ε. Calibrated noise is added to every statistic the generator draws from a profile, and the report states what the noise dropped.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepTags.descri: 🏷️ A tag is one org-wide label with a fixed meaning, applied to sources, tables, columns, relationships or commands. Tags change behavior, and a tag can require a reason, an expiry date or a parameter when it is applied.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepTags.title: Tags carry meaning
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepTestDataMap:
Safe, realistic data to build and test against comes from four parts, each with one job:

  • Environment: a branch of the model. At creation it inherits its parent's connections or starts unbound, and you point its sources at your own databases.
  • Profiler: measures real tables, giving the shapes everything else is built from.
  • Fakes: in test data, a column's fake replaces its identifying values.
  • Synthetic data: fills a non-production environment with generated rows shaped like the profiled tables.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.stepTestDataPro: 📊 A Data Profiler measures the tables you add to it: column shapes, distributions, value frequencies and children per parent. Fill from profile turns those measures into fakes, and a synthetic dataset draws its rows from them. Watching the same runs for drift is covered in the Data quality Deep Dive.
What fakes and synthetic data are built from
de/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontAnaly: The BI side reads as analyst: it sees every order, but no customer's email. The SQL explorer now runs as analyst. Late shipments by region and carrier, over the same tables and relationships. a_customer shows an email masked, as the analyst reads it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontApp.d: This is the sample app's order-history screen, rendering that answer for the demo's signed-in customer: seven orders, their lines with product pictures from MongoDB, and delivery status from the shipping service. The app holds no joins and no access rules; the model holds both.
