de/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontBi.de: Apache Superset connects over the PostgreSQL wire protocol, with the PostgreSQL dialect: host and port of Provisa's pgwire server (5439 by default), database provisa, user analyst. It browses the shop's tables and views and charts revenue by region and late shipments by carrier from the same model.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontCatal: Each product is a MongoDB document, with its name, category, price and picture. Provisa reads it as a table.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontEvery: Next, the role picker switches back to All. The BI side reads as its own role, which is chosen where its SQL runs.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontJsonA: A client that prefers JSON:API asks for the same orders, still as the customer, with their lines and shipments included. Each order links the lines and the shipment it includes, and a line's id is its composite key.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontPoint: SHIPPED_AS joins an order to its shipment. The app and the BI tool both read through it and every other relationship, under the same rules, so the customer sees their own orders and the analyst sees no emails. Change a relationship or a rule here, and both consumers have it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontRelat: OF_PRODUCT joins an order line in PostgreSQL to its product in MongoDB. With PLACED_BY, HAS_ITEM and SHIPPED_AS, these four relationships are declared once, and both the app and the BI tool read through them.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontScena: A coffee retailer serves two consumers from one model. Its app's order-history screen shows a signed-in customer their orders, and its BI tool charts revenue and late shipments for the analysts. The orders are in PostgreSQL: customers, orders and each order's lines.
One model, an app and BI
de/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontScree: The app sends its queries as the customer role, whose row filters limit every answer to the signed-in customer's own orders. The role picker is now on customer. The order-history screen sends this one nested GraphQL query for each order with its lines, each line's product from the catalog, and the order's shipment from the shipping service. Run as customer, it answers seven orders, all the signed-in customer's own.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontShipp: Each order's shipment comes from the internal shipping service over REST, read through its OpenAPI document, with the carrier, the tracking number, and when it was promised and delivered.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingAnswer: orders_last_five_minutes is a materialized view of each region's orders and revenue over the last five minutes. Every batch of orders that lands refreshes it, so you're reading stored rows a few seconds old, never the topic itself. Run it again in a minute and the numbers will have moved.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingCached: The same view in GraphQL. @cached(ttl: 10) asks for the response cache. The same question within ten seconds is answered from the cache, and the X-Provisa-Cache header says HIT.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingCatalo: catalog is the shop's Postgres, with what each product is and costs and the regions the shop sells in.
The latest orders in the table, a few seconds behind the topic.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingJoin.d: PLACED_IN joins each order to its region, and ORDERED to its product, so an order's revenue comes from the catalog's price.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingLive.d: A GraphQL subscription on the orders. Every batch that lands sends the latest orders again. Leave it running and watch the list move.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingOrders: orders is the topic, landed into its own table as the orders arrive. Every batch that lands refreshes the views that read it and notifies their subscribers.
A Kafka topic landed as a table and joined to the catalog. A view stayed current with every batch that landed. The same answer came back in SQL, GraphQL and REST, cached when asked, and a subscription followed the feed. Look around on your own from the query page.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingRest.d: The same view as a REST call, for a dashboard that polls it.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingScenar: A coffee shop's orders arrive on a Kafka topic, a few a second, and its catalog is in its Postgres. The shop wants to know which regions placed the most orders in the last five minutes. orders is the broker the orders arrive on.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataCoverag: Before pre-prod existed, the coverage check listed every sensitive column and whether a fake covers it. Here customers.email has none. A Test (fake) environment refuses to open, and refuses every read, while a sensitive column has no fake. Once the steward declares one, the column is covered.

Sensitive coverage is a standard report on the Reports page: each sensitive column, its tags, and whether a fake covers it, read now from the model. Every one is covered, so pre-prod opens and answers.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataDev.des: Every row in dev was generated from production's profile, with the same columns, value shapes and spread, and none of the real rows. When even pre-prod's real rows can't leave production's boundary, give testers this synthetic copy.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataDevAnsw: The same view in dev. The regions and categories are the ones production has, and the totals are close to production's without being its numbers.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataDevGrap: Each order with the customer who placed it, through the relationship. Keys were generated to line up across tables, so every API reads dev as a consistent dataset.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataDone.de: One model, three environments. Prod holds the real rows. Pre-prod reads them with every sensitive column faked, for every role. Dev is generated from production's profile and holds nothing real. Fakes are declared once per column, and an environment that would show a sensitive column unfaked refuses to open.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataPollyPr: Polly is asked which fake it would propose for customers.email. It reads the column's latest profile run, sees that the values are email addresses, and proposes the email fake. The model already declares one, so the proposal checks that choice against the data. Nothing is saved until someone chooses to.
A fake proposed from the profile
de/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataPreprod: The same customers, read in preprod. Each name, email, city, sign-up date and customer number is a fake, computed as the row is read. The region is real. Pre-prod reads production's own data through Provisa, and the only identity that connects to production's stores is Provisa's own. Nothing is copied out.

The same view in preprod gives exactly production's revenue by region and category. Every real row, volume and edge case is there for final testing. The customer number is faked the same way on customers and on orders, so the joins still match.
As analyst, or as any other role, pre-prod's sensitive columns read as fakes. No grant, mask or role shows the real values in a Test (fake) environment.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataProd.de: In prod you see the real customers.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataProdAns: Revenue by region and category, from the real orders.
The generation report compares each generated table with the production profile it was drawn from, column by column: distributions, null rates, distinct values and how columns move together. It shows how close dev is to production, without showing production.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataScenari: shop-db is a shop's production database: customers, products and orders. Teams need data to build and test against. Here one model serves three environments. prod is the real rows, the source of truth, and nobody builds against it. preprod is production's own data with every sensitive column faked, for final testing. dev is generated from production's profile and holds nothing real, for everyday building.
Three environments over one production database
On customers, the name, email, city and sign-up date each declare a fake, and so does the customer number: an identifier, and the sign-up date a quasi-identifier that could single someone out. Region, products, orders and amounts declare none, so they stay real. Which columns to fake is the operator's choice, made once in the model.
The model says which columns are faked
de/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataToDev.d: Next, the switcher moves to dev, a Test (synthetic) environment.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataToPrepr: Environments are branches of one model, as in git. Next, the switcher in the header moves to preprod, a Test (fake) environment.
Next, the switcher returns to prod.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.vulnerabilities: One alert for each pinned package version with a published advisory, naming the repository, the package, the CVE, the version that fixes it, and whether the alert is open, fixed or dismissed.
The Dependabot alerts

The view exploited_in_our_code is stored. It keeps each open alert whose CVE is in CISA's catalog, with the number of days since CISA's due date passed. Internet-facing repositories come first, then the ones longest overdue.
The answer in SQL
Grouped by team on the server, the same view shows how many exploited vulnerabilities each team has open, and how long the oldest has been overdue.
The answer in GraphQL
The government data comes from AskAmerica: the NVD's CVE records, MITRE's catalog of software weaknesses and CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities.
The public vulnerability data
Cypher shows the same joins as a graph of repositories, the open alerts raised in them, their CVEs and the catalog entries that mark them exploited.
The answer as a graph
A CVE record and its entry in CISA's catalog share the CVE identifier, and this relationship joins them. With the alerts joined to their CVEs, an alert reaches the catalog in two steps.
Exploited, by CVE
Each CVE that attackers are known to exploit, with the date federal agencies must fix it by and whether ransomware campaigns use it.
CISA's known exploited vulnerabilities

The NVD holds a quarter of a million CVEs, and the company's alerts name nineteen. The table's landing filter, a condition on its own columns, keeps only those when the table is landed, so the replica holds just the records the alerts need.
The CVE records, landed through a filter

You saw the company's own code data joined by CVE to public vulnerability data, only as much of it as the alerts need. One view in one governed model answers which exploited vulnerabilities are in the code and how overdue each one is, in SQL, GraphQL, Cypher and REST.
What you saw
The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped and counted on the server. A ticketing system or a dashboard gets the answer without writing SQL.
The same answer over REST

A software company wants to know which of the vulnerabilities in its code attackers exploit, and how long each has gone unfixed. Its repositories, their packages and the Dependabot alerts on them are in its own database; the CVE records and CISA's catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities are public. The tour shows Provisa joining the two by CVE and answering the question in SQL, GraphQL, Cypher and REST.
What this demo is

The company's ontology defines known exploited vulnerability, CVE, CWE and CVSS, and ties each term to the columns it describes. A CVSS score says how severe a vulnerability is. Only the catalog says whether anyone is exploiting it.
The vocabulary
de/tour.json::tour.steps.weblogsDone.des: Three sources became tables, joined on a request id, and answered the shop's question in SQL and over REST.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.weblogsJoin.des: nginx gives every request an id, and the shop names each database connection after it. The LOGGED_FOR relationship tells Provisa to join a statement to its request on that id, so no query has to spell out the join.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.weblogsLogFiles: The shop has three sources: shop-db, its PostgreSQL database, and two log sources, shop_access and shop_db_log. Provisa reads each log file where it sits, one line to a row.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.weblogsRest.des: This REST call returns the slowest pages again, each path with its request count and its average and longest time. Every surface Provisa serves reads the same governed model, so REST gives the answer SQL or GraphQL would, under the same rights.
A small web shop wants to know which pages are slow, and which SQL makes them slow. The answer is split across nginx's access log, the database's statement log and the shop's own database. The tour shows how Provisa reads log files as tables, joins them across sources and governs them by role, then answers the question in SQL and over REST.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.weblogsStatemen: The slowest pages joined to the statements their requests ran, in plain SQL over two of the demo's views. A view is a saved query that Provisa expands into this statement before it runs. Here is where the time went, statement by statement.
The SQL behind a slow page
de/tour.json::tour.steps.weblogsTables.d: Each source's data is registered as tables: the shop's customers, products and orders, and one table for each log, with its lines split into columns such as path, status and time. On top of those, two views add the slowest pages and the SQL each request ran. A view is a saved query.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupAlias.d: These are the names that differ from their member's name. Germany FR and West Germany are Germany, Zaire is DR Congo and the Soviet Union is Russia. Each match was reviewed before this demo froze it, and 27 of the 237 were corrected. A team whose results passed to no member keeps its own name. East Germany stays East Germany, so its 1974 match against West Germany is not Germany against Germany.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupByConfe: Grouped by confederation, UEFA's members hold 13 titles and CONMEBOL's hold 10. No other confederation has won a final.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupDisagre: Counted by the names Wikipedia writes, Germany has one title and West Germany three, as if they were two countries. Kaggle writes the same team as Germany FR, so a join on names between the sources misses those titles too.
Every final from 1930 to 2026, with the winners and runners-up by the names of their day. Wikipedia lists the 1954, 1974 and 1990 titles under West Germany and the 2014 title under Germany.
The finals, as Wikipedia lists them
de/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupFunctio:
country_alias is a Python source, and this function is the table every cross-source relationship joins through. It receives each team name the sources write, asks an LLM which FIFA member the name stands for, with a key from the organization's vault, and returns the member's name and FIFA code. It runs again on its refresh interval, so a new name is matched as it appears.
def country_alias(name: str) -> list[Alias]:
    """The FIFA member a team's name stands for: West Germany and Germany FR are Germany.

    @table
    """
    reply = anthropic.Anthropic().messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
        max_tokens=2000,
        output_config={"effort": "low", "format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": ANSWER}},
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": ASK + name}],
    )
    match = json.loads(next(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text"))
    return [Alias(name, match["canonical_country"], match["fifa_code"])]
de/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupGraph.d: Each member links to the finals it won, under whatever name it won them. Germany's node holds 1954, 1974, 1990 and 2014.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupGraphql: In GraphQL each final has a winner field through country_alias, so 1954, 1974 and 1990 read West Germany beside the member they stand for: Germany, GER.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupIntro.d: Who has won the World Cup, and from which confederation? The answer is spread over public data: Wikipedia's list of finals and its confederation articles, and two Kaggle datasets of every World Cup match and every international goal. Each source names countries its own way. Wikipedia writes West Germany, Kaggle writes Germany FR, and the confederations' member tables write Germany. This tour sources the data, makes the names agree with a short Python function, and queries the result as one governed graph.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupIntro.t: Four public sources, one World Cup
de/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupJunctio: WON joins a confederation's member to the finals it won through country_alias. The member's FIFA code finds every name it stands for, and each name finds its finals. RUNNER_UP, PLAYED_HOME, PLAYED_AWAY and SCORED join the same way.
This is a Kaggle source, the FIFA World Cup dataset, with every tournament, match and player appearance from 1930 to 2014. Each of its files arrives as a table. A second Kaggle source holds every international goal since 1916. Like the Wikipedia tables, they are public data, registered in minutes and governed like any internal database.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupMatches: Kaggle writes West Germany as Germany FR and East Germany as German DR. A few of its names carry stray markup from the file, such as rn">Republic of Ireland. The file's blank lines are kept as rows with no values, as the dataset has them.
Matches by the names of their day
de/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupRecap.d: Public data from Wikipedia and Kaggle, sourced in minutes and governed like any internal database, made to agree by about ten lines of Python and queried as one graph. The function's matches were reviewed, so the graph counts every title once, under the right member.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupSql.des: The same join in SQL counts each member's titles through country_alias. Brazil leads with five, and Germany and Italy have four each.
de/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupWikiped: This is a Wikipedia source. Its crawl reads seven pages: the List of FIFA World Cup finals and the articles of the six confederations. Each data table on those pages becomes a table named by its page and its caption, so the finals are list_of_fifa_world_cup_finals__list_of_fifa_world_cup_finals. A public source is governed like any internal database, with the same roles, grants and masks. Set a refresh interval and these sources stay current on their own. This demo reads a fixed snapshot, so every visitor sees the same answers.
